Arvind Krishna & Nikesh Arora: Quantum Threat, Open vs Frontier AI, AI Cyber Warfare & SaaS Collapse

TL;DR

Quantum computing poses a severe, imminent threat to global cryptography by around 2030, necessitating an immediate enterprise shift to post-quantum infrastructure. Meanwhile, the AI landscape is shifting toward open-weight models and task-specific optimization over costly frontier LLMs, driving massive SaaS consolidation.

Quantum Computing & Cryptography

  • The 2030 Threat Timeline: Arvind Krishna states that the DARPA Quantum Benchmarking Initiative (QBI) midpoint points to roughly 2030 for quantum computers to break today's cryptography.
    • Stolen Data Risk: An encrypted hard drive stolen today can be stored for 5 years and broken once quantum machines reach scale.
    • Enterprise Unpreparedness: Nikesh Arora warns that organizations are already late, as 3-5 years is insufficient time to overhaul IT stacks, noting that ~50% of current infrastructure spend is not quantum-safe.
  • Evolutionary Milestones:
    • Error Correction: Krishna predicts demonstrations of error mitigation/correction on running quantum computers by 2027.
    • Scaling Qubits: Moving from current toy computers (~10,000 physical qubits) by adding a zero per year could reach ~10 million qubits by 2029.
    • Logical vs. Physical: Arvind Krishna clarifies that error correction decreases effective capacity, yielding a much lower number of "logical" qubits (e.g., 10,000 physical yielding ~200 logical).
  • AI vs. Hardware for Code-Breaking: While an AI model might theoretically discover a new number theory algorithm or prime number distribution to break keys, Krishna notes it cannot run efficiently on classical architectures (GPUs/arithmetic) without actual quantum hardware.

Open-Weight vs. Frontier AI Models

  • The Economics of Tokens:
    • High Costs: Frontier models cost $20 to $50 per million tokens, making them economically unviable for universal enterprise traffic inspection (e.g., inspecting endpoint traffic).
    • Open-Weight Cost Reductions: Arvind Krishna notes that running an 800-billion parameter open-weight model (like Kimikay 3) on optimized in-house GPUs with a week of engineering drops costs to $1–$2 per million tokens—a 10x to 40x reduction for 95% of capability.
  • Strategic Deployment Paradigms:
    • Phased Adoption: Arora notes enterprises are in a discovery phase where employees use the best available models to understand capabilities, but will transition to task-specific Small Language Models (SLMs) trained on proprietary data.
    • Exceptions for Frontier Models: Frontier LLMs will be reserved for high-stakes scenarios where potential business disruption justifies the cost—such as deploying agent swarms during an active cyber breach.
  • Geopolitics and IP: Krishna projects that 75% to 90% of token usage will shift to open-weight models driven by economics, IP/brand protection, and geopolitics (with the gap between Western and Chinese open-weight models closing to 6–12 months).

AI in Cyber Warfare & Security

  • Asymmetric vs. Symmetric Defense:
    • Defensive Scaling: Krishna outlines that warfare principles require technological superiority and symmetric costs; defenders must make security as cheap as attacks by pooling vulnerabilities and sharing automated patches across trusted industry alliances.
    • Vulnerability Asymmetry: Nikesh Arora notes that AI-driven tools (like Mythos) can spot vulnerabilities, but attackers only need one exploit while defenders must patch every flaw. Early testing shows AI security outputs have a 60% to 80% real-flaw rate alongside 20% hallucinations.
  • Agentic Code Generation: Krishna states that agents now write roughly half the code inside his organization, producing superior results because agents can execute evaluations and fixes before deployment. However, fully verifying the correctness of arbitrary input code remains computationally infeasible.

Geopolitics, Regulation, and the Global Arms Race

  • The Inevitability of the Arms Race: Panellists agree that global AI development cannot be slowed down; if Western nations or specific states attempt bans or heavy restrictions, countries like Japan, China, and India will accelerate to capture market advantage.
  • Data Center Backlash: Arora highlights local political populism driving discussions of extreme measures (like hypothetical 50-state data center bans), though uniform adoption across all 50 states is unrealistic.
  • Compute Access Divide: Arora warns that the primary global divide will not just be economic, but based on supply constraints of compute—leaving companies further from the epicenter (e.g., in Europe) at a structural disadvantage.
  • Capital vs. Labor: Krishna notes that historical cycles favor capital-intensive nations over those bogged down by left-leaning philosophies focused on protecting every existing job rather than adapting to labor displacement.

Vertical Integration & SaaS Consolidation

  • The Modern Conglomerate and Infrastructure:
    • IBM & Nvidia Parallels: Krishna compares modern vertical integration to the historic IBM mainframe (controlling the stack from chip design to software) and points to Jensen Huang at Nvidia as managing a modern vertically integrated stack "down to the dirt" to control profit pools and commoditize layers.
    • Application Layer Moots: Arora argues that application providers will build vertical stacks integrating software, reasoning, memory, and context, creating high friction and sticky moots for personal and enterprise agents.
  • Enterprise Software Consolidation:
    • SaaS Disruption: Arora predicts massive disruption in the SaaS space over the next 5 to 8 years as AI transforms software product-market fit.
    • Vendor Reduction: Krishna notes enterprises currently use 500 to 5,000 distinct software vendors; AI capabilities will drive massive consolidation down to 5 to 10 main platforms to reduce attack surfaces and distribution costs. Non-interaction-rich systems (like core banking database lookups) will resist easy AI replacement.

Predictions & Forward Calls

  • Quantum Threat Timeline: A quantum computer capable of breaking today's cryptography will emerge around 2030 (Midpoint of DARPA QBI timeline) — Arvind Krishna.
  • Error Correction Milestone: Someone will demonstrate error mitigation or correction on a running quantum computer by next year (2025), with verified progress by 2027 — Arvind Krishna.
  • Qubit Scaling Target: Quantum computing capacity will scale by adding a zero per year, reaching 10 million physical qubits by 2029 — Arvind Krishna.
  • Open-Weight Token Dominance: Between 75% and 90% of all enterprise token usage will go to open-weight models within 1 to 2 years — Arvind Krishna.
  • Geopolitical Gap: The capability gap between Western and Chinese open-weight models is 6 to 12 months at the most — Arvind Krishna.
  • SaaS Market Disruption: There will be massive disruption and consolidation in the SaaS space over the next 5 to 8 years, replacing hundreds of disparate software vendors with 5 to 10 main platforms — Nikesh Arora & Arvind Krishna.

BlackRock’s Fink Sees Inflation Risk in Slow Data-Center Buildout

Bloomberg Television(3.3M)·10:27·2026-10-21
Larry FinkCEO, BlackRock Francine LacquaAnchor, Bloomberg Television
TL;DRLarry Fink warns that delays in building data centers could drive up computing costs and jeopardize economic growth.
He also notes that historic competition for capital—driven by federal deficits and massive AI investments—will likely keep term premiums elevated. Competition for Capital: Larry Fink notes a historic level of competition for capital, fueled by cumulative federal deficits in the...

TL;DR

Larry Fink warns that delays in building data centers could drive up computing costs and jeopardize economic growth. He also notes that historic competition for capital—driven by federal deficits and massive AI investments—will likely keep term premiums elevated.

Capital Competition and Macroeconomic Pressures

  • Competition for Capital: Larry Fink notes a historic level of competition for capital, fueled by cumulative federal deficits in the U.S. and scaling deficits in other democracies.
  • Crowding Out and Term Premiums: Private capital is finally being unlocked, but concurrent demands—such as hyperscalers requiring $7 to $9 trillion in the U.S. alone for AI buildouts—are pushing term premiums higher.
  • Global Debt-to-GDP Strategies:
    • U.S.: Requires 3% annual economic growth to shrink the debt-to-GDP ratio.
    • Germany: Currently sits at a 60% debt-to-GDP ratio, where Fink suggests more fiscal stimulus could lift GDP.
    • Japan: Faces a 230% debt-to-GDP ratio and an aging population, making the rapid adoption of robotics and AI essential to increase productivity and grow out of debt.

AI Infrastructure and the Economic Risk of Delays

  • Deflationary Impact of Data Centers: Fink argues that a slower buildout of data centers is actually more inflationary because current computing costs are so high; faster construction yields more compute and brings down costs.
  • Economic Jeopardy: With roughly two-thirds of U.S. capital expenditures tied to technology (cloud, AI, and competitive CAPEX), slowing the infrastructure buildout threatens the broader economy.
  • International Competition:
    • Canada: Marc Carney spearheaded permitting reform allowing a one-year federal, provincial, and local permitting term, with plans to build 20 gigawatts of renewable power in Nova Scotia and Newfoundland.
    • Global Destinations: India and Abu Dhabi are also positioning themselves as major hubs for data center development, meaning if the U.S. fails to build locally, the infrastructure will be built elsewhere.

Political Gridlock and Public Sentiment

  • Legitimate Local Concerns: Fink agrees with politicians who argue that data center developers must secure their own power, avoid taxing communities, and deploy closed-loop water systems rather than draining local water supplies.
  • Public Fear: Post-midterm leadership must address widespread public uncertainty and fear regarding job security, food inflation, and housing inflation by providing clear, hopeful visions for the future.

Long-Term Investing and Market Noise

  • The Cost of Timing the Market: Citing S&P performance over a 25-year period (6,300 days), Fink notes:
    • Doing nothing yields an 11% compounded return.
    • Missing just 10 days drops the return to 6%.
    • Missing the top 40 days results in a negative return.
  • Global Asset Management Activity: BlackRock is engaged in deep discussions regarding data center financing and workforce trust-building.

Retirement Innovations and Global Mandates

  • LifePath Paycheck: BlackRock created this product to provide retirees with a steady paycheck from defined contribution plans, which Fink expects will become the default product for DC plans.
  • Dutch Pension Transition: The Netherlands is moving away from government-oriented defined benefit plans to defined contribution plans, awarding BlackRock an $80 billion contract as the preferred vendor to manage the shift.

Societal Blessings of Technology and Demographics

  • Technological Milestones: Smartphones emerged in 2012, and global connectivity tools like Starlink now enable communication anywhere in the world, including Kenya.
  • Labor Shortages and Productivity: Both Germany and the U.S. report 4% unemployment alongside massive labor shortages. Fink asserts that without changes to immigration policies, societies must rapidly adopt robotics and AI.

Notable Quotes

*"The faster we can build out more data centers, the more compute we have, the faster we can bring down the cost."* — Larry Fink

>

*"If we don’t build out these data centers, it is actually more inflationary because the cost to compute is so high right now..."* — Larry Fink

>

*"If you invested in the S&P over the last 25 years and you went on vacation for 25 years... you would have earned an 11% compounded return. If you were out of the market for the 40 top days out of 6,300 days, you had a negative return."* — Larry Fink
First of all, let’s start with markets. Markets, okay. Where do you see interest rates going? I think there’s a huge competition, as I wrote in an op-ed last week, that there’s huge competition for capital. We are starting to see the effect of this cumulative of of our federal deficits in the U.S. We’re starting to see the impact in other democracies, that the scale of the deficits are are are becoming crowding out. We’re at a time now where we’re finally unlocking private capital, and so the competition for capital is is as large as I’ve ever seen in my professional career. If you listen to the hyperscalers in the United States alone, they’re talking about a need for $7 to $9 trillion to build out and the be and to ensure that the United States is a leader in AI. That type of financing, that type of funding on top of the financing for the federal deficits is is putting the term premium to be higher, and I think we’re going to see that term premium higher. In addition, there’s a push and pull in this. If we don’t build out these data centers, it is actually more inflationary because the cost to compute is so high right now and the faster we can build out more data centers, the more compute we have, the faster we can bring down the cost. So, the irony, in the short run, people are frightened of of the impact of data centers in their community, much of it is misinformation, but but the but the tech companies and the builders have to do a better job working alongside each and every community. Larry, last week, I mean, you were saying that a moratorium on data centers could could put the country in a recession. Are we really that dependent? About two-thirds of the U.S. economy’s capital expenditures right now on on technology, whether it’s cloud, or whether it’s AI, whether it’s just the CAPEX of making making sure that you’re competitive. And if we slow down the build-out of this technology, I think it really does jeopardize the economy. It means we’re not going to build these. It means we’re building them elsewhere. So, there’s a lot of fears going on and it’s and everybody’s saying I can’t control this, I’m frustrated, I’m frightened. Well, as you know, you know, we’re the largest retirement manager in the world. We focus more on the long-term, we’re not focusing on the day-to-day. I don’t care what the markets are doing. I don’t focus on the ups and downs at all. I think it’s real noise. I’m an interesting fact that I I like to tell everybody. If you invested in the S&P over the last 25 years and you went on vacation for 25 years and you learned how to be the best rock climber or the best whatever you you you wish, you would have earned an 11% compounded return. 11% doing nothing by enjoying your life. If you were if you believed you were smarter than the market and you were out of the market for 10 days, just 10 days, your return was down to 6%. If you were out of the market for the 40 top days out of 6,300 days, you had a negative return. And so all this tells me is all this ups and downs and noise, what’s happening, it doesn’t truly matter for the average person. Larry, even global bond yields, because there’s there’s alarm bells, they’re they’re flashing something, and at some point, will it not come to roost? They’re flashing that they’re saying, okay, wake up federal government. Our deficits are starting to have real large issues. What I tell every politician, we need to grow our economy by at 3% a year to make the debt to GDP to shrink. Look, but each country has different issues. We’re sitting here in Germany. They have a debt to GDP of 60. I could sit here and talk to the federal government here and say, I’d be doing a little more fiscal stimulus to you, you know, to they’re really get this economy going and it finally is starting to lift GDP. But in Japan, I’d be telling the political leadership embrace the new technology. You have a debt to GDP of 230%. You have a very fast aging population. If you adapt quicker than any other nation in terms of robotics and AI, you are going to increase productivity and you’re going to grow out of the problem of your debt to GDP. So, there’s not one solution that’s fitting any one nation, and and I think we have to look at this and try to come up with the best strategy for each and every country. I know last week on the earnings call, you said something that got people talking, Larry. As always, you said, “BlackRock is in the market with a major transaction.” What it Can you clarify? Is it a a an extra data center? We’re we’re involved in more and deeper conversations than we’ve ever had in the history of the firm, whether it is working with the hyperscalers or related to the financing of data centers, but we’re working with other companies on how to how to how to how to rebuild trust with their workforce. There are many areas in the country where their workforce only has a defined contribution plan, they don’t understand it, they don’t understand what that means when they retire. We created a product called LifePath Paycheck where the where the participant gets a paycheck when they retire. And that is having a huge impact on the future of retirement, having people have more security when they have retirement. And I believe this will become the default product for defined contribution plans. But even in places like Netherlands, you know, they’re moving away from the traditional government-oriented defined benefit plan to a defined contribution plan, and BlackRock was awarded as the preferred vendor this $80 billion contract to move the Dutch pension fund community from DB to DC, and now we’re trying to help them understand that. How how does AI actually change the way we’ll retire? I mean, how much do you think about the fact that our societies will change fundamentally with AI and so the way we invest, the way we consume, the way we will retire changes? Technology changes shape our lives in so many wonderful ways. I mean, I think think about your life before you had a smartphone. A smartphone was created in 2012. It wasn’t that far ago and now it is the most important device in your lifetime. Ignorance was bliss. Ignorance was bliss. Now think about, okay, if you travel to Kenya and traveled around the world, you’re not now in an area where you can’t communicate with everybody.   • AGI Status: Chamath Palihapitiya asserts that AGI has already been achieved, but its diffusion is bottlenecked by physical infrastructure build-outs rather than the underlying technology.
  • Anthropic's Public Benefit Fund:
    • Subject to stockholder approval, Anthropic has committed 5% of its shares (estimated at $75B–$100B based on a $1.5T–$2T valuation) to a public benefit fund, with an extra 2% added for every 50% increase in valuation.
    • Alex Wissner-Gross views this private fund—rather than direct public distribution—as a "snub" to universal basic equity and the current administration.
    • Chamath criticizes traditional philanthropy and the Giving Pledge as reputation washing, arguing high-achieving individuals should deploy capital directly rather than handing it to unknown administrators.
  • Espionage and Security at Labs:
    • Federal authorities arrested Abdul Rahman Alfonso, an OpenAI engineer accused of planting a USB recording device in an executive conference room.
    • Chamath notes that tech giants like Meta should assume foreign nationals among thousands of employees are exfiltrating data, framing this as a standard corporate reality.

Wealth, Philanthropy, and Economic Restructuring

  • Elon Musk’s SpaceX Gift:
    • Musk announced he will give one SpaceX share to every American child under 18 (72 million kids, totaling roughly $10.5B, or about 1.1% of his stake) via Trump Accounts.
    • The panelists agree that asset ownership beats cash handouts, with Dave Blundin emphasizing that teaching a generation to own equities prepares them for an AI-driven economy where value shifts from paychecks to assets.
  • Capital vs. Labor Taxation: Chamath argues that capital should be taxed progressively higher while labor should potentially not be taxed at all, shifting the burden onto the 99th percentile of wealth creators and acting as a check on fiat currency debasement.
  • National Debt and the AI Lever:
    • Elon Musk stated that the $40 trillion national debt cannot be solved from within the government and will instead require AI and robotics to drive economic growth and efficiency.
    • Chamath and Salim Ismail note that GLP-1 weight-loss drugs, cancer vaccines, and robotic productivity can dramatically lower healthcare and government costs, effectively rebasing the debt relative to a much larger GDP.

Post-Capitalist Economics and the Energy Constraint

  • Energy as Currency:
    • Elon Musk predicts that conventional fiat currency will become irrelevant, replaced by fundamental physics metrics like power (watts) and tonnage (mass and energy).
    • Chamath reveals he has locked up nearly 6 gigawatts of power, envisioning a future where value is tied to embedded compute and energy resources, traded via crypto tokens representing access rights.
  • The Compute and Power Bottleneck:
    • Chamath warns that enterprises not named OpenAI, Anthropic, or the hyperscalers will face multi-year wait times for cloud and launch capacity, forcing terrestrial builds, local VPCs, and air-gapped facilities.
    • Alex Wissner-Gross points to model distillation and recursive self-improvement as counter-forces that will drastically reduce the energy footprint of future models.
  • Idea Generation vs. Execution: Bill Gross launched Idealab.ai, a free platform providing 1.2 million AI-generated business ideas. Chamath remarks that business ideas are a dime a dozen and that startup success is entirely about execution and personal grit.

Crypto, Markets, and Investment Strategy

  • Bitcoin and Crypto Outlook: Chamath states that traditional crypto is "capped" because fiat-centric institutions lack fungibility, user privacy creates severe security/kidnapping risks (citing France), and future AGI reasoning traces could theoretically break SHA-256 and target Satoshi's wallet. He predicts Bitcoin will eventually get hacked and go to zero.
  • Index Funds and Free Cash Flow: Chamath advises ranking the Global 2000 by free cash flow yield and buying the top tier, as traditional S&P 500 concentration makes broad index diversification unreliable.
  • Silicon vs. Data Centers: Chamath avoids investing in chip startups due to saturated fab space and memory blockages, preferring to play the infrastructure stack at the data center level (power and infrastructure) and the application layer.

Predictions & Forward Calls

  • Elon Musk claims SpaceX will become worth orders of magnitude more than the current Earth economy, with valuations reaching 1 to 10 quadrillion dollars.
  • Alex Wissner-Gross predicts that within 30 years, current economic units like energy, land, and power will look unrecognizably different, and society will laugh at today's currency discussions.
  • Chamath Palihapitiya predicts that traditional crypto assets will eventually get hacked by advanced AI models and go to zero.

Citadel CEO Ken Griffin Says AI ‘Almost Certainly’ in a Bubble; Trump Has 'Mixed Scorecard'

Bloomberg Podcasts(600.0K)·48:53·2026-10-21

TL;DR

Ken Griffin says investors are "almost certainly" in an AI bubble, likening GPU overcapacity to the 2000 telecom fiber glut, while warning that U.S. fiscal deficits and inflation threaten living standards unless the nation bets heavily on productivity and robotics.

Artificial Intelligence & The Market "Bubble"

  • Paradigm Shift in White-Collar Work: AI models can now complete high-level PhD and master's-level tasks in hours that previously took 4 to 6 weeks, threatening traditional white-collar jobs and eliminating corporate competitive moats.
  • GPU Overcapacity Risk: Griffin compared GPUs to the airline industry and the 2000 telecom fiber buildout, warning that marginal pricing will go into freefall if provisioning exceeds demand, upressing 7-to-9 year chip capitalization assumptions.
  • Corporate AI Spending Rationalization: Sophisticated companies are increasingly utilizing open-source models at a fraction of the cost for routine tasks, becoming much more selective about paying high prices for state-of-the-art models from OpenAI and Anthropic.
  • Bubble Parallels: Griffin stated there are "almost certainly" bubbles within this technological transformation, drawing parallels to the 1999–2000 internet boom where enduring market leaders emerged on the other side.
  • Citadel's Alpha Generation: Core research at Citadel remains fundamentally human-driven, with portfolio managers assembling narratives based on TAM, unit economics, and management incentives, while trading execution has become the most heavily automated and technologically advanced component.

U.S. Fiscal Policy, Tariffs & Economics

  • The "Spending Orgie": Griffin noted the U.S. spent as much money during the pandemic relative to GDP as it did to win World War II, leaving the country without sufficient fiscal space to renew tax cuts.
  • Disastrous Tariffs: Griffin criticized tariff battles with Canada, Europe, and allies as a "fiasco" that has proved pro-inflationary and severed global supply chains.
  • National Debt and Bond Markets: With the federal deficit at $40 trillion, multi-decade high bond yields are flashing warning signs that the U.S. needs to put its fiscal house in order or face higher inflation, a weaker dollar, and falling living standards.
  • Growth via Productivity: Griffin emphasized that the singular economic focus must be growing the economy through the AI revolution, data centers, nuclear fusion/fission, batteries, and robotics.

Political Landscape & Elections

  • Trump's Mixed Scorecard: Griffin evaluated the Trump administration's record as a "mixed scorecard," praising border closures but criticizing the handling of the war in Iran, immigration enforcement for established workers, and inflationary tariffs.
  • Midterm Warnings: Griffin warned that if Republicans take a beating in the upcoming midterms, leaders in the House, Senate, and White House must listen to voters rather than doubling down.
  • The French Socialist "Nightmare": Griffin pointed to recent turmoil in France—where the government spends 60% of GDP—as a warning against safety-net-rich socialist policies, comparing the resulting societal breakdown to his experiences looking out his Chicago window.
  • Education Reform: Griffin highlighted the failure of public schooling (noting 53 schools in Illinois without a single child at grade level) and praised high-performing alternatives like Eva Moskowitz's Success Academies in New York.

Corporate Culture, Robotics, & Geography

  • Carnegie Mellon Robotics Gift: Griffin recently gave a $3 billion gift to Carnegie Mellon University to fund its leadership in robotics, aiming to reindustrialize America via factory automation rather than low-value manufacturing.
  • Miami Expansion and Cuban Ethos: Griffin described Citadel's center of gravity as "somewhere over the middle of the Atlantic Ocean" (between London, Miami, and New York), while praising Miami's pro-business environment and the anti-socialist ethos driven by its Cuban immigrant community.
  • In-Office Collaboration: Citadel maintains a strict in-office policy where teams are kept in single geographical locations, relying on physical whiteboards and face-to-face mentorship to develop younger talent.

Predictions & Forward Calls

  • *None in transcript*

Notable Quotes

"As a business owner, you're seeing your competitive moats be filled in by bulldozers. And then at the same time, you're thinking that this will be a golden era for entrepreneurs."

— Ken Griffin

"The big picture is there's almost certainly bubbles within this moment in time. And, and any radical transformation of our economy is generally intertwined with a bubble."

— Ken Griffin

"Everyone's favorite go-to answer when they're losing money is hedge funds are deleveraging... The reason that people love that answer is it actually washes your hands of accountability."

— Ken Griffin

"France is the dream that the left talks about, the liberal, safety net safe safety net-rich socialist Europe, and here's France. That dream, that dream is the nightmare I left from Chicago."

— Ken Griffin

TL;DR

Citadel CEO Ken Griffin stated that investors are "almost certainly" in an artificial intelligence bubble amid questions over long-term GPU demand and corporate spending efficiency, while warning that U.S. fiscal deficits and inflation threaten the economy unless policymakers prioritize productivity growth.

The AI Transformation, Corporate Spending, and Market "Bubbles"

  • Paradigm Shift in White-Collar Work: Ken Griffin described a moment of initial depression upon realizing AI models can solve PhD-level finance and research problems in hours that previously took teams of PhDs four to six weeks.
    • *Economic Impact:* Griffin noted that AI threatens traditional white-collar roles while simultaneously creating a "golden era" for entrepreneurs and startups that hire workers with non-traditional pedigrees.
    • *Reskilling Need:* Griffin emphasized that the U.S. lacks actionable national programs to reskill workers displaced in fields like translation.
  • Alpha Generation vs. Research: Fundamental-based investing and research remain the core of Citadel's business, which Griffin likens to journalism.
    • *Automation:* While AI aids with bits of research, the narrative and valuation multiples are still assembled by humans, whereas the *trading* execution side has become the most technologically automated part of the firm.
  • GPU Overcapacity Concerns: Griffin drew parallels between modern GPU deployments and the 2000 telecom dark fiber bubble and the airline industry.
    • *Margin Risk:* If the provisioning of GPUs eventually outpaces demand, marginal pricing could enter a freefall, complicating capitalization rates and revenue models for chips.
  • AI Bubble Realities: Griffin confirmed that the market is "almost certainly" in an AI bubble, echoing historical transformations like the internet boom and railroads where the underlying technology permanently changes daily life despite initial market corrections.
  • Corporate ROI Realities: Companies are becoming increasingly discerning about their software spend, balancing high-cost, state-of-the-art frontier models from OpenAI and Anthropic against cheaper open-source models.

Portfolio Restructuring and Market Volatility

  • Situational Awareness Trade: Citadel stepped in to provide a holistic solution for situational awareness, acquiring a complex portfolio overnight in under 24 hours to help the firm raise cash and protect substantial year-to-date gains.
    • *Market Dynamics:* Griffin noted the portfolio was caught in "three midsize storms" (including Kimmy model announcements, foundational model growth chatter, and pension portfolio reshuffling) compounded by fast-money accounts front-running anticipated distress.
  • Hedge Fund Deleveraging Myth: Griffin dismissed the common media narrative that market sell-offs are primarily driven by "hedge fund deleveraging," calling it a convenient excuse that stops investors from doing rigorous underlying research.

US Midterm Elections and Political Landscape

  • Midterm Power Dynamics: Griffin views the upcoming U.S. midterms as a traditional check and balance, predicting Republicans will almost certainly lose the House and/or Senate.
  • Mixed Policy Scorecard:
    • *Foreign Policy & Immigration:* Griffin criticized the administration's handling of the Iran war explanation and immigration policies, while praising the rapid closing of borders as a major win.
    • *Tariffs & Inflation:* Griffin labeled tariff battles with Canada, Europe, and allies a "pro-inflation disaster" that severed global supply chains.
  • The "Socialist Dream" Warning:
    • *French Protests:* Griffin pointed to recent turmoil in France—where the government spends 60% of GDP—as a nightmare warning against progressive policies.
    • *Domestic Concerns:* He cited Illinois Governor JB Pritzker and progressive policies as moving America down a dangerous path toward excessive taxation, corruption, and unsustainable spending.

Fiscal Policy, Deficits, and Economic Growth

  • The National Debt & Fiscal House: With the federal deficit reaching $40 trillion and pandemic spending matching World War II levels relative to GDP, Griffin warned that high 30-year bond yields reflect a bond market signaling that U.S. fiscal governance is disordered.
  • The Growth Solution: Griffin argued that the only way out of entitlement crises (Social Security, Medicare, Medicaid) and deficits is economic growth driven by productivity.
    • *Priorities:* To spur growth, the U.S. must embrace AI data centers, nuclear fusion and fission, battery technology, and robotics (highlighted by his $3 billion gift to Carnegie Mellon University).
    • *Education Reform:* Griffin stressed fixing broken K-12 education systems, praising Eva Moscowitz’s Success Academy model in New York.
    • *Global Alignment:* Griffin argued the U.S. should use political capital to push European allies to enact meaningful economic reforms (such as longer working hours) rather than relying on American defense while capping workweeks.
    • *Immigration of Talent:* Griffin advocated granting green cards automatically to elite international graduates from U.S. colleges.

Citadel Culture and Geographic Footprint

  • Center of Gravity: Citadel’s operational center of gravity exists "somewhere over the middle of the Atlantic Ocean" between London, Miami, and New York.
  • Physical Proximity: Griffin emphasized that Citadel keeps its internal verticals geographically clustered because physical presence, whiteboards, and person-to-person interaction remain crucial for mentoring young talent and driving collaboration.

Notable Quotes

*"You're seeing the threat to white collar jobs playing out as a business owner. You're seeing your competitive modes be filled in by bulldozers. And then at the same time, you're thinking that this will be a golden era for entrepreneurs..."* — Ken Griffin
*"Everybody's favorite go-to answer when they're losing money is hedge funds are deleveraging. In fact, in the last 10 years, I've seen the entire industry deleveraged to zero at least 10,000 times... The reason that people love that answer is it actually washes your hands of accountability."* — Ken Griffin
*"Here's France that dream that dream is the nightmare I left from Chicago. That dream doesn't belong in our country... an economy, a society where where it comes down to how much you can take from others—and they'll first take your property and then they'll take your personal rights—that's not a society that we want to create..."* — Ken Griffin
*“We're not going to get out of these waters by torturing each other. We're going to get out of these waters by making the pie bigger for all of us."* — Ken Griffin

David Qian / ECOVACS: Father & Son, Inside Business Succession, Robotics, and My Search for Meaning

TL;DR

David Qian, CEO of ECOVACS Robotics, reflects on succeeding his founder father, navigating the transition from a traditional manufacturing background to global tech branding, and managing the delicate balance between personal desire, organizational capability, and the realities of leading an A-share listed company.

Background, Succession, and the Father-Son Dynamic

  • Upbringing and Path to Succession:
    • Born in 1990 in Shenzhen; spent his formative years split evenly between Shenzhen (until age 11), Canada (ages 11 to 22), and his return to China at age 22.
    • Sent to Canada abruptly at age 11 by his father via a notification rather than persuasion, experiencing a largely independent, "free-range" upbringing.
    • Joined ECOVACS in 2012 directly after university, initially working on e-commerce and manufacturing production lines without an explicit, premeditated succession plan.
  • The Father-Son Relationship and Leadership Handover:
    • His father built ECOVACS brick by brick as a traditional manufacturing entrepreneur, later launching the *Tineco* brand as a second venture while stepping back from day-to-day management of the core business.
    • Unlike expectations of receiving constant life wisdom or mentorship, his father's training style was decidedly hands-off: assigning difficult tasks and letting him learn through trial and error.
    • Reflecting on second-generation identity, David views the company not as his own founding "child" (like entrepreneurial peers Wang Xingxing or Liu Jingkang), but as a shared family responsibility and extension of his life's work.

Going Global and Overcoming Strategic Missteps

  • Early Breakthroughs in International Markets:
    • Tasked with turning around the overseas business around 2015 when overseas subsidiaries were losing 50 million yuan.
    • Shifted strategy from traditional local general-manager sales models to leveraging domestic e-commerce operational capabilities directly on platforms like Amazon.
    • Achieved rapid success, capturing roughly 30% market share in the German market within six months, proving the viability of high-value-for-money Chinese hardware going global.
  • The CEO Slump and Organizational Tuition Paid:
    • Became CEO at age 29, initially experiencing a false peak of life before hitting severe organizational friction.
    • Attempted to merge domestic and international divisions prematurely ("like oil and water"), causing business growth to stall.
    • Realized his Western management theories and business textbooks clashed with the reality of a traditional, 20-year-old Chinese private enterprise culture; recognized that he had "overestimated himself and underestimated the competition."

Product Strategy, New Categories, and AI Perspectives

  • Agrarian vs. Nomadic Business Philosophy:
    • Describes ECOVACS's approach as an "agrarian civilization"—planting seeds, farming carefully, and enduring loneliness—rather than a "nomadic" grab for meat across unrelated trending sectors.
    • Core innovations include pioneering the all-in-one docking station with AI vision and voice in 2021, a product architecture that still defines the robot vacuum industry standard.
    • Expanded multi-category offerings around household needs, achieving 2 million unit shipments in window-cleaning robots and scaling robotic lawn mowers and pool cleaners.
  • Rational View on Physical AI and Embodied Robotics:
    • Maintains a grounded, pragmatic stance on AI hype, noting that while to-B industrial robotics may land in 3 to 5 years, consumer home robotics will likely require a 10-year horizon.
    • Argues that humanoid robots and embodied AI are currently in an era of "using a very big hammer to hit a very small nail," and emphasizes that ECOVACS will pursue its own methodical pace rather than blindly chasing market bubbles.

Company Metrics, Targets, and Future Goals

  • Global Revenue Share: Overseas revenue currently accounts for 50% of total business and is projected to reach 60% to 70% over the next few years.
  • Core Operating Principles for Competition: To succeed against intensified rivals (such as Roborock and Dreame), a company must execute three things well: see far, run fast, and make fewer mistakes.
  • 10-Year Vision (2018–2028): Aiming to complete the transition from a single-category floor-cleaning specialist into a fully internationalized household brand providing diverse robotic "butler" solutions.

Predictions & Forward Calls

  • David Qian predicts that overseas revenue share will reach 60% to 70% within the next few years. (Attributed to David Qian)
  • David Qian estimates that commercial and factory applications for embodied AI will land within 3 to 5 years. (Attributed to David Qian)
  • David Qian projects that consumer-facing home robotics applications will require a 10-year process to fully mature. (Attributed to David Qian)

Notable Quotes

"I've always described us internally, I said we are actually more like an agrarian civilization, not a nomadic one. We like to bury a seed and farm the land and let the crops grow. Nomadic is another way of doing things, right? The industry is big, I'm going to take a bite of the meat." — David Qian
"When you think you're so awesome, you're really not far from being an idiot. Really just a fine line apart. And I think the more awesome you think you are, the faster you enter the idiot stage." — David Qian
"A company generally won't run into huge problems if you do these three things relatively well: whether you see changes clearly enough, whether your management can make this body run strongly enough, and avoiding fatal mistakes." — David Qian

Today, if people look at and truly understand Ecovacs, they'll find we should be the most complete in the industry, able to cover the household needs of global consumers with all kinds of robots, not just a company that only makes robot vacuums. Actually, in the years after Ecovacs went public, competition in the whole industry wasn't that strong. Right. But later, with Roborock... Right. ...emerging. Right. going public, and including Dreame — competition actually intensified further. Right. How do you view this batch of competitors, and how do you respond to them in competition? Companies of each era are different. It's still that saying: a company is a product of its era. This batch of the era's — let's say, new founders or new companies — the resources and elements they command may be different from the ones you're familiar with. So the competitive environment you face is completely different. Right. The competitors are completely different. But this is your heavy responsibility, right? It is. You have to see it clearly yourself. Right? If I only lived in the era when the company originally grew and in the elements built in that era's environment, I think even if you fully mastered let's say, the elements the company built in that era, it wouldn't necessarily succeed in the next era. Each era is somewhat different. The elements are different. So I think this is actually a responsibility and challenge for me. Right. How do you think you've performed in dealing with their competition in the past? There was good and bad, I'd say. Do you think you overestimated the competition or underestimated it? I think I overestimated myself and underestimated the competition. Why did you overestimate yourself? I think to a certain extent I do understand my own shortcomings, right? Confidence and arrogance may be just a fine line apart. So I think I still overestimated myself. But I don't think I need to feel inferior either. Once you figure it out, it's actually all fine. Right. How will you deal with competition going forward? First of all, competition is always there. Competition won't, because of you — especially in this industry — competition won't cease to exist because of anything you do. Yes. Right? Competition is always there. In this process, you need to — actually, I think for a company it ultimately comes down to three things: First, whether you can see far. Second, whether you run fast. And I think the third is that you don't make mistakes. A company generally won't run into huge problems if you do these three things relatively well. Most situations arise from these three things, right? For example, whether you see changes clearly enough, see your own capabilities clearly. What we call running fast is your company's ultimate execution, right? Whether your management can make this body run strongly enough. The third thing, I think, is what we call the inner issue: that is, your pursuit of reasonable desires and the restraint of unreasonable desires — the relationship between them. Many companies make mistakes. Making mistakes is actually the biggest fatal wound. So you think this competition ultimately all comes back to the company itself? You think it has nothing to do with these external competitors? Do you analyze them? I think I do look, and after looking, in the end you find it's just about what you need to improve and adjust. You can't envy... When you work out, you can't envy someone's great body while you don't exercise and still eat junk food — what's the use? Right? If you believe you can do it, just put it into action. It's not that hard. And then, step by step — discipline, step by step, based on your goals, take real action and achieve your goals. Mm, has competition ever really troubled you? Being troubled means not being able to figure it out. It's just not figuring it out. It's just — in the end you find it's just that you hadn't figured it out. If you figure it out and actually know how to change, I think it's all fine. I think a company had best follow: 70 to 80 percent is replicating your capabilities and 20 to 30 percent is improving capabilities. I think many times people might hope for 70-80% improvement and 20-30% replication. Actually, replication itself is the process of you expanding and getting stronger. Like we said, exercise itself is actually doing enough repetition. Right? Then you master that skill and capability. I think today Ecovacs, in our strategy execution, does exactly this — we don't overthink having some powerful, earth-shaking change in capability in the short term. I think we should do the replication that should be done, while following, say, the reasonable boundaries of your industry. So actually today, I think in our choice of industry and choice of market, we are following this path. I think in the end it comes back to this: you'll actually find that the process of a company's development isn't just one straight road and one destination. It actually involves certain choices and certain twists and turns. So it's hard to say that, you know, I have a rival and this rival is my goal. I don't think a rival is your goal. Right? I mean — and in most cases, this life-or-death struggle — I can't see what it ultimately becomes. Look at the so-called, in China, what we've seen: so many well-known companies going head-to-head and nothing much came of it. They're each still around. Tempering each other, steel against steel, I'd say, making themselves better. I think it's that kind of process. It's not a company's development goal. A rival is not a company's development goal. It exists, and you have to respond, and in this process, you have to make yourself better. It's a touchstone. Right? The goal is still your company's own vision for the future, including the things you hold on to. I think that is the goal. For example, what do you think of Yu Hao? I don't have any particular view. He just exists. Right. Mm. Creating user value — that's what I think is most core. Consumers actually never like anything mentally taxing. I'll say it again: the best way to do right by consumers is to truly deliver what they expect — the results. Because I think the products we make — actually, many times newly created categories haven't been standardized or defined — you have to define them. It's not like in the past, when this thing was already defined — you have to define it. I think this is of course a very exciting thing. You can constantly, based on the elements of industry innovation, constantly define better products. But within this, it's a constantly cycling process. Consumers give you feedback. Actually, the globalization we just talked about is the same — global consumers are actually very different. I think the future competition of Chinese companies must be global competition. It's about who can do global competition better, earlier, and better. In a reasonable state, Chinese companies should only — I mean, revenue from the China market might be just 30%. So there's actually a huge market space overseas. But then, how do we understand overseas markets? You actually find that global consumers differ greatly. So I think this is actually one of the most critical things for a company's development. What do you think is the core moat of consumer electronics? There's no core moat. No core moat? What core moat is there? I think... Brand might be... Brand, I think, is just the consumer's perception from their last purchase of your product, helping them quickly decide on the next purchase. But if your next delivery isn't good, then it's not a moat anymore. Yes, mm. Right? I think it's just a memory. Of course, it depends on what it is — for example, Coca-Cola never changes its taste. OK, but in consumer electronics nothing stays the same forever. Right? Water never changes; many things can stay unchanged. They can create permanent memories, or very long-lasting memories. But consumer electronics is changing. I think it can only be said: today a consumer bought this product, and it created a memory of your brand, which might help him make a choice next time. But by the next choice, the consumer electronics industry will have changed. So next time, if you've changed for the worse, then... this memory, I think, just comes to an abrupt end. So it's definitely not brand. Then what could it be? I think it depends. I think you — you could say Apple definitely has one, right? But there are also many — I think even the vast majority of consumer electronics doesn't. Apple's — its existence is based on its network effect, to a certain extent, right? But actually, if consumer electronics is pure hardware, there's no network effect — it's just a scale effect. Right. So this doesn't really exist. So you don't try to build a moat? Investors all hope you have a moat, right? So you can keep making money endlessly. But the only real moat is monopoly. Honestly, to a certain extent, in today's world of rapid change and explosion, monopoly is very hard to form — theoretically it can't exist. So I actually think companies can only relatively find your scale effect. But — not many companies can necessarily build a moat. Mm, so in this process, you have to quickly find your own scale effect. Iterate — the speed of iteration, right? I think that's all there is. I think I'm a fairly realistic person. I find it hard to rashly say, OK, hey, I'm building a moat — this moat comes from Ecovacs' brand and our so-called understanding of global consumer households. Yeah, you could say it that way, but — it's not necessarily true. Many companies might choose to say these things, but I don't think it's true. How do you win in competition? See far, see clearly, run fast, restrain desires, make fewer mistakes. What's your biggest mistake? In the past few years? I think it was having desires that didn't match our capabilities. But you just said your directions were right. Right. The so-called mismatch is where capabilities didn't match. It's not necessarily the desires — it can be the capabilities that didn't match. Then you need to improve your capabilities. Right. Not necessarily change the desires. Mm, right. I think the direction wasn't wrong — it's the capabilities. Just change the capabilities. Have the capabilities changed now? Have they improved? I think there's definitely been change. But nothing is absolute. At the end of 2022, ChatGPT came out. AI large models actually began to change the entire industry. How do you view this new technological change? Since a company is also a company of its era, in the next era, what do you think Ecovacs will do? I think there are two aspects. One is how your company, with such a technological change — I think for a company, first let's split it in two: there are two kinds of impact. One impact is today's model-based AI Agent, right? The way your company operates and manages, the changes it can produce. And then there's your product, right? One is your way of operating, the other is the direction in which you can generate revenue. I think today let's talk about the second one first, right? First, we can see that in the past few years, the ones actually generating positive revenue are the ones making industry infrastructure companies. Suzhou has many of them too. Actually making things like optical modules, right? All these various things — I mean, what we call the whole token infrastructure business. That's definitely not our industry. So what we can still choose is today's what we call Physical AI, the embodied AI thing. Of course, I think looking at it from this angle, I think we look at it the same way: if we look at a 10-year horizon, first, I think today, using the whole large model and including the embodied AI thing, I estimate that within 3 to 5 years there can be some commercial and factory applications. I estimate. But we do to C — we serve consumer household needs. I think that should be a 5-to-10-year process. Of course, if we look at a typical startup — it's really hot right now, right? Unitree also took 10 years to go public. So actually I think this might be a 10-year process. So within 3 to 5 years, if it's to B, to-factory, to-industry demand, I think that one has the conditions to land. Because I think robots, in daily life or rather in applications, what they can best replace are the jobs where today you train people more to become like robots. They're highly standardized and don't demand such strong generalization ability, I'd say. But if we come back to the home, we actually believe that, whether hardware or software, the conditions for maturity are still some time away. So I think for me, if we put this on a 10-year cycle, I would more think — I'm not exactly saying — that Ecovacs needs to be overly urgent today about making some embodied robot to bring into the home, because it's not realistic. But we will, in this industry process — and we've always thought of ourselves this way: we are a company transforming from making tools to making a kind of butler robot in the future. So I think this is what we call what this whole era brings — if we're talking about Ecovacs' entire products and the change in the direction of your revenue generation. The other one is the organization. I think everyone has talked a lot about this too, right? The changes AI brings to organizations today. As a company, we certainly think about it this way too and we're also practicing it. So I think... today internally, our consensus on this matter is roughly this. Do you think in the future Ecovacs will be a manufacturing company or an AI company? I think the products and industry we're in today aren't built entirely on manufacturing genes either. You inherently have to use innovation to define consumer needs or to explore consumer needs, and use innovation to satisfy them — that itself is technical work. It's not that you're just relying on large-scale manufacturing's cost reduction or efficiency to do better. I don't tend to think a company needs such an absolute definition in this regard. No need, I think. Many car companies are already spinning off their embodied AI — that's one path to choose. Right? I mean, the industry has hype today, right? What we call heat — there's heat, there's a bubble. Yeah, you could say that, right? Actually everyone is working in one direction. Honestly, there's no essential difference. I just don't think there's an essential difference. Anyway, everyone rushes in. In the end you'll find there's not much difference. I think today, in China's supply chain, putting together a robot isn't too hard. Right? Putting together a robot in Shenzhen isn't too hard. I even think a leading embodied-AI company could sell you one, and you could package it as Ecovacs — that probably wouldn't be hard either. Right now this industry is actually still a case of taking I think a very big hammer to hit a very small nail. Of course, I think there's nothing wrong with using a hammer to hit a nail. That is to say, many companies started out like this too, I remember. I remember back then, actually, when drones first came out nobody was sure what exactly this thing could do. There was a French company called Parrot. Back then they were probably on par with DJI, maybe even earlier. At that time, that company later chose I think they once partnered with Walmart to turn it into a toy. Of course, that nail may have been the wrong one to find, right? DJI, in the end, chose to position itself as what we call prosumers — the so-called semi-professional consumer scenario. Right? And it eventually became a productivity tool. That nail was probably a better find. So today, actually, the whole embodied AI field — I think it's all a process of holding a hammer and looking for nails. Searching here and there — I don't think there's much difference; everyone's doing it. They say they're going for the home, but in the end they all end up in factories. You feel this isn't the most important thing for you at this stage? I don't think this is absolutely the most critical thing for us at this stage. If it were, I think we'd definitely have to think about how to carve out a path of our own. Because being the same as everyone else — there's no essential difference. That's meaningless, hmm. Right? Everyone doing the same thing, right? And others may have more of a comparative advantage in this competition, right? Say you're a startup — you don't have to worry about delivery, revenue, or profit. You just need to put out papers and demos. Right? Another case is, you'll find listed companies doing it or big companies — unless they're of absolute scale, with truly, so-called spare cash to do this kind of thing. But I saw XPeng just spun it off too, right? XPeng doesn't have spare cash to do this either, you know, or he has to think about how his investors face this matter. He also hopes to raise more outside capital. Right, right? He can't possibly drive this with his own capital. He must have made a choice and a decision on this. And startups are also better at allocating interests to the core team. Right, so there are really only a few paths to choose from here. If you do the same as everyone else today... But I don't think this is something that we need, today, to make a judgment on. Yeah, we can wait a bit. Although we ourselves make robots, and we also hope that in the future, in 10 years, Ecovacs can develop in robotics. That's for sure — I don't think that goal has changed. I think it's just that we ourselves need to explore a path of our own, right? Following the hype, I mean, I don't think that's where our comparative advantage lies. But you also just said you think Ecovacs should do things like a farmer tilling the land. Right. Then it needs to start early. So today, is everyone nomadic or farming? Today it's nomadic. Right? Everyone thinks this is a piece of meat, everyone thinks it's easy to raise money in the primary market, thinks this is a good direction for startups — that's nomadic, right? I think so. Right? So if it's farming, I think we're definitely doing some things. For example, we're working on things like "Bajie." We definitely have R&D investment in this. We also, definitely — including investing in the supply chain, making some key investments and laying out positions. But I don't think it's something we need to scramble for meat over today. There's nothing — what meat is this meat? So far I haven't seen where the meat is. This meat is illusory. Everyone is describing a — I mean, you know — With cars, you have something comparable and referenceable. Back then, the annual car ownership in China was right there. Electrification replacing gasoline and gas power. That's completely comparable data, right? And cars didn't become more numerous because of it. There was just substitution happening within it. But how do you quantify the meat of embodied AI? People can now imagine it's a new market. Right, yes, it is a new market. It is a new market, but how big is it? It could be infinitely big in the future, right? Because we're talking about replacing humans, right? It could be infinitely big in the future. But if — but I think at that stage, you'll actually find that this market, for a company's valuation — roughly how big can it get? Today Unitree is at 200 billion. China's most valuable company is at 4 trillion. Suppose this is the most important industry of the future. Investing in Unitree today, say... Let's assume any random individual, hmm, right? Then it grows 20x. Of course, maybe it exceeds 4 trillion. Right? But as I keep saying, I think people are very enthusiastic about the changes technology brings. But how big a thing it ultimately becomes actually has to go through quite a long process before it lands. Take autonomous driving. Yeah, I often observe on the road how many consumers today are using autonomous driving in all scenarios? I mean, every car sold has it — everyone talks about this feature. It's an old car from over ten years ago. And looking at it today, autonomous driving globally is actually worse than in China. China is already a leader in this accelerating space. Actually, not that many. So I think I'd rather think about this question more rationally. What do you think the path that belongs to Ecovacs might look like? Do you have some ideas now? You don't want to do the same as them, homogenized? First, I think if we look at it, I mean, first, China's future supply — the hardware supply capacity will be very abundant. So actually, maybe — I think in terms of hardware, the whole industry chain should be very rich in the future. So the thing you master — what's the key thing you really need to master? Maybe it's — you know — maybe software. But with software, as we also know, if you want to build a world model today, the investment is huge. It's just huge, right? And actually everyone's doing data collection today, right? And the standardization of data collection is iterating fast, right? A data collection method from maybe a year ago might not even be useful by now, right? Yesterday — a couple of days ago I just saw Figure released an app, saying everyone come do data collection. So I think the whole industry is still in a genuinely early stage. I think for us, it's about choosing a reasonable pace. If and when we see hardware and software able to land in commercial scenarios to a certain degree, and moreover, I think it's with high robustness, replicable and scalable, then by that time it won't be far from home use. And at that time, I think for us it would be a very reasonable thing. In your imagination, do you think this wave of AI or intelligence-driven home appliances will undergo huge changes? Home appliances have been intelligence-driven for years. They've all been said to be intelligence-driven, right? TVs have AI, air conditioners and fridges have AI. But I think consumers are very rational. One is, in the process of competition, everyone talks about this thing. But when consumers finally pay with real money, I think they're still quite rational. In the end it still comes down to whether the value for money you deliver is good. Our products all have AI in them, all empowered by it. Of course — robot vacuums need to avoid obstacles. Our robotic lawn mowers need obstacle avoidance, object recognition — things that help improve efficiency — it's always been there. But I think — many people also ask me once embodied AI comes out, will Ecovacs as a company cease to exist? Right? Because it feels like a straight replacement. But I actually think, by the time it develops to that stage, robot vacuum penetration should be quite high. People shouldn't be at the point of having your robot where you'd need to buy a vacuum cleaner for your robot. It shouldn't come to that. Right? Including today, for example, us doing robotic lawn mowers overseas. Consumers have effectively already replaced the push mowers. So when embodied AI comes in, it shouldn't be that for this robot they'd buy another push lawn mower. Right. Right, so I think actually I personally lean toward thinking about robots as a bit like Darwin's theory of evolution. In the future there will surely be all kinds of robot species. And they'll evolve deeply based on their scenarios to reach the optimal experience or fit for that scenario — the capabilities they grow. Of course, maybe there will be ones with two hands and two legs, humanoid beings. But there will also be, I think, very many other kinds of robots. That would probably be a relatively reasonable state. Relatively diverse. Because we too — we humans are just one species in the natural world. Right. Never the strongest, either. So I think that's a relatively reasonable state. So you will, at what you consider the right pace, do future product definition. Do you think Ecovacs will cease to exist in that era? Do you feel pressure? Do you — I think ceasing to exist has many other reasons and factors. It's not that in this era it's solely because of this change. You don't think it's brought about by technological change? Technological change is very important. Right, but that's just that's just some companies failing to keep up with the times. Right? and some other key factors. I think it's just that — it's not absolute. It's not like once it appears, you're gone. Robots are also divided into the brain camp and the body camp. You definitely belong to the body camp, right? If you do it, would you go into the model layer? I think not at present — we haven't entered models. Have you tried investing in any models? No. I think we're probably better at product definition, thinking about consumers based on — us understanding consumers' needs at home, what exactly they do. Is your attitude toward AI relatively on the conservative side? I think the impact it brings definitely exists. That's beyond doubt, I mean, yes. Whether for individuals or industries, it exists. But whether within a very short time it produces earth-shaking change — I lean toward looking at it more rationally. So far, what I've perceived, or what ordinary consumers have perceived — I don't think it's brought decisive change. You know, before Sam Altman talked about AGI. Now he doesn't talk about it anymore. Right? He's off doing coding too, right? Back then when he talked about it, it felt like, wow, it's over, like superintelligence was coming any moment — now that doesn't exist either. Of course, in some places you can indeed feel it. If AI today could do this kind of AGI capability — actually making videos and content is already strong, right? We're still talking face to face, right? Yes, your content product is still a key, necessary existence in the content ecosystem. It's not like it completely replaces today's creators and they're gone. It just gets generated and they're gone. People will use this capability to make improvements. I think... People still like to watch human content. I think so too. Of course people, you know, used to say maybe AI-generated content wasn't good enough, right? too AI-ish, and then they keep making it better and better. But you have your own judgment too. People still like watching people, still like human content. If a consumer sees an embodied robot dancing outside, what does the consumer see? There are lots of these on the street, right? I think what they see is just a spectacle. They find it interesting that it can wave at you. Ordinary consumers are really like this. Of course — I think practitioners have a kind of sentiment, right? Our drive for technology, our drive for industry change. That sentiment is important. I think desire is important — I'm not saying desire is bad. Desire is important; it's a powerful driving force. Right. It makes the world change in some way. But I think today, you say the Spring Festival Gala has a bunch of robots dancing — what change do consumers feel? What change to their lives? Hmm, as for doing real work, it's still a desert. Ha, right. I hope one day, of course, it will absolutely be like that — I hope one day and I also hope Ecovacs is a key player in that, able to bring a robot into consumers' homes. At our core, we make these products hoping to help consumers solve problems — no doubt, we hope to save their time. I've always believed one key thing we actually do is not just helping everyone sweep the floor clean or mow the lawn well. At the core, it's even about saving them time. With embodied AI like this, such robots appearing in the future — I think that's of course great. We can free up more of consumers' time. But whether it's something that will appear tomorrow — I don't — I absolutely don't think it will appear tomorrow. I mean, is this restraint, pessimism, or conservatism, or is it just rationality? Do you think this wave of technology could possibly take Ecovacs to the next level, the next rung of the era? The possibility? From that angle, shouldn't you embrace it more actively? I think all companies probably think this way. Right? So actively embrace it — but I think when running a company, when doing corporate governance and management today, there must be a right pace — it's not I think, just emotional wishful thinking. As I just said, maybe it's just personal imagination — I have a facing a huge incoming wave, we can change dramatically, earth-shaking. That's of course a matter of desire, I think — not a mistake either. It's a correct direction. But when doing it, I think you still have to think about the steps. Right? Which steps are reasonable? Can they be what we can do today, what we can bear? I think this is a balance. You've also lived in Suzhou for exactly 14 years now. Right. Do you like this city? I always thought you were from Suzhou. Only today did I find out you're not. This city is interesting — historically it hasn't had natural disasters. So I think it nurtured some local culture. I personally feel you rarely meet Suzhou people around the world or even across China. Suzhou people don't go out much; they mostly live in Suzhou. It was a land of fish and rice, relatively wealthy. Right? They never felt the need to flee or expand outward. It really is, I think, a culture at Suzhou's foundation. It's also — to some degree I sometimes feel it's quite like Canada — pretty laid-back. It's not like Beijing, Shanghai, Guangzhou, Shenzhen, a particularly, particularly excitable city. But Suzhou is also important. Suzhou is still one of China's top industrial cities. And actually, looking at today — today's Suzhou, whether it's robotics, there are very many companies. Including what we just talked about, AI infrastructure — there are also many companies here in infrastructure. It's a place where you can work with peace of mind. Less hustle and bustle, but very solid. Working with peace of mind. You think Suzhou is quite like your personality? Maybe, ha. But I'm not sure if it's from living here so long that I became like this, or I was always like this. That I'm not sure of. As the CEO's brain, do you feel you've now connected with the company's capillaries — connected? Already connected. Right. As you go deeper into this company, the longer it gets, do you feel you understand your father better? Of course. I think getting to know — He's an entrepreneur, right? This was built by him. A company. For a long stretch of his life, his dedication to this was extremely strong. And I don't think that will change much. Something you've been used to for decades is very hard to change. So I can understand his love for his own enterprise. So what do you think your responsibility is? As a second-generation successor? I'm also one with this company now. I've invested such a long time and dedication into it, right? I'm not something separate from it. I definitely'm merged into one with it. Just like the many long-serving employees in the company. It's actually part of everyone's life. It occupies my life, my own personal — I think my spiritual investment is also in it. Hmm, you've grown together with it. Right, there's no way to separate — you definitely. So your mission, as one of the company's key managers today, is to make this company develop better and better. Just now you didn't seem to tell me what your desire is — a desire from the heart, right now. Actually, running a company or being a CEO, on this road there's no retreat, right? You can only do better and better. Getting better and better is a kind of desire. Of course. You could also stay in place. Staying in place means getting worse and worse — you're all racing. You can only get better and better. But how do I quantify it? Me saying I become number one in the world, or whatever rank. Honestly, I think that kind of thing is pretty hollow. Right? Is it important? Many companies are already number one globally. Their entrepreneurs are still working, still striving. Right? So your desire, in some sense, ultimately is self-actualization, self-fulfillment, right? Whether you can keep setting goals, setting difficulties for yourself or face difficulties based on goals that you must overcome. Your desire or sense of achievement comes from that. I think maybe I've seen a lot of it in my father. You know, I remember maybe at 40 he told me he'd retire. At 50 he told me he'd retire; at 60 he told me he'd retire. And you find he just can't seem to stop. So even if you set a limit for yourself or a goal of your own, once reached you're still thinking what's next. Sometimes, actually, when you've reached a peak you feel, I've got it all. When you're the CEO, often you actually quickly lose, I think, — most of it, actually, you see. I mean, if everyone feels they've gotten what they deserve, and then I've hit my goal, then actually you'll slack off, you'll lose the sense of the next goal. What often greets you next isn't more gain, I think it's more loss. But I think this is also part of understanding him. You realize that someone who's always been fighting just keeps fighting. Do you enjoy the fight? I don't think I used to be a particularly fierce person. It's the same point: you may have a lot already, so there's no need to struggle and... Right. fight and grab. Right. But I think I do have it. You were sparked by the environment. Yes. People are creatures of their environment. You were sparked these past few years. I think it's gradually solidifying, or becoming an increasingly core part of me. You can't say it wasn't there before. If it really wasn't, I could have just not come to work, just lie flat. You must have had some desire, to some degree, wanting to gain something. But it grows more and more with the process. I think all entrepreneurs are like this. Who says on day one, "I want to—" They just have a small goal, achieve a small stage, then define the next stage of growth and goals, then achieve that. I think it's all like this.
