TL;DR

Demis Hassabis reflects on his journey from a chess prodigy and 1990s video game designer to co-founding DeepMind and winning a Nobel Prize, emphasizing the need for societal collaboration and rigorous standards to safely steward AGI into the world.

Early Life, Decision-Making, and Video Game Design

  • Chess Foundations:
    • Learned chess at age 4 after watching his dad and uncle play; was beating them within a couple of weeks and went on to captain England junior teams.
    • Relies on a chess-like approach to real-world decision-making: gathering as much information as possible and working backward from a desired goal through strategic mental simulations.
  • Ignored Advice:
    • During a postdoc at MIT, classic AI professors dismissed deep learning and reinforcement learning as bad ideas; Hassabis listened to their reasoning, disagreed, and pursued it anyway.
  • Multidisciplinary Roots:
    • Designed the hit 90s video game *Theme Park*, which pioneered detailed simulations down to individual visitor behaviors and emergent phenomena (e.g., visitors eating burgers after fast roller coasters and feeling sick).
    • Believes the best work happens when technical fields collide and collaborate with the arts and humanities (noting his family is entirely on the arts side).

DeepMind: Founding, Google Acquisition, and Scientific Impact

  • Founding DeepMind (2010):
    • Launched in 2010 when AI was considered a niche or dead end, helping seed the modern AI industry.
  • Google Acquisition (2014):
    • Sold to Google for around $650 million after Larry Page reached out (facilitated by investor Elon Musk and other backers).
    • Triggered by the need for massive compute—orders of magnitude beyond what a small startup could access—and a due diligence "Rubicon moment" where top Google researcher Jeff Dean reviewed DeepMind's code.
    • Does not regret the valuation despite hindsight, maintaining the primary goal was advancing the mission of safe AGI and scientific breakthroughs rather than maximizing financial wealth.

AI Risks, Guardrails, and the Future of AGI

  • Critical Warning Shots:
    • Recent reports of AI agents hacking companies and governments are serious warning shots demonstrating the need for proper guardrails and secure testing environments.
  • Frontier AI Standards:
    • Advocates for establishing a standards body to test and certify frontier AI systems.
    • Expresses concern over future risks spanning cybersecurity, biology, and nuclear domains as systems become significantly more powerful over the next 1 to 2 years.
  • The Most Pressing Question:
    • The core challenge is how to safely steward AGI into the world and determine what society wants an AGI-enabled future to look like.
    • Urges society—including philosophers, artists, and humanists—to debate and chart this future rather than leaving it solely to technologists.

Nobel Prize Recognition

  • The Stockholm Experience:
    • Received the unexpected call from Sweden at home while working, causing his normally relentless brain to go completely blank in shock.
    • Followed in the footsteps of childhood heroes like Richard Feynman and 1920s/30s physicists, culminating in a week-long celebration in Stockholm in December.

Notable Quotes

"I'm not very good if I don't have some problem to solve, so fortunately there's a lot of problems." — Demis Hassabis
"If we hadn't sold at that time, we wouldn't have been able to go on and do some of the great scientific work we ended doing." — Demis Hassabis
"I would probably say, strangely, to believe even more in the strange ideas that kid had... And then maybe the second thing would be to say, maybe have a little bit more fun on the way, because it will turn out okay in the end." — Demis Hassabis
The thing about being in my head is that there's never an off switch, so it's quite tiring as well. I'm not very good if I don't have some problem to solve, so fortunately there's a lot of problems. Welcome to your job interview. Great to be here. You are, resume speaks for itself. Chess prodigy at 12 years old, designed and programmed the 90s video game, Theme Park, and of course, co-founded DeepMind, which would go on to create AlphaFold, win you a Nobel Prize, and lead you to found another company, Isomorphic Labs. What is the first thing you remember being good at? Oh, wow. So I think it was probably when I was about 4 years old, learning chess. So I saw my dad and my uncle play. Apparently, I asked them, could I, could they teach me, so they humored me, but then after a couple of weeks, I was beating them both, and then they took me to the local club, and then I ended up, you know, capturing all the England junior teams after that. What is one piece of advice early on that you are glad that you ignored? I don't know if I ever ignored pieces of advice, I kind of try and solicit as much information as I can and then kind of synthesize that and then make my own decision. I do remember during my postdoc at MIT, talking to some of the big names, big professors in classic AI, and asking them about this idea of, you know, building learning systems with deep learning and reinforcement learning, and they thought it was a very bad idea. But when I listen to why they thought it was a bad idea, I didn't really agree with their reasons. So I thought, at least if it didn't work, as we were thinking about setting up DeepMind, it would not work in an interesting new way. How do you go about making a decision? It sounds like that synthesis of information is really interesting. Maybe it comes to my chess background of like trying to get as much information as possible, obviously in the real world you can't have perfect information, unfortunately, like a chess game, but you can try and get as much information as possible, and sort of, you know, almost, try and play out in your mind, strategize in your mind, a plan back from the goal that you want to achieve. What are the intermediate steps? Every choice you make in the real world is very complex, there are always, you know, pros and cons to it, and I think you just got to make the most of the, of the plus sides of it. But you love a simulation. I do. Any, any type of simulation. I think those have been my two, passions in the beginning really is AI, and then, simulations, and, and often combining the two. What do you view as the most consequential decision of your life thus far? I think my whole life's been a series of, kind of maybe a little bit unusual or slightly unconventional decisions. I'm not afraid of doing those. I guess if I was to think what's the most consequential is probably starting DeepMind in 2010 where pretty much nobody thought AI would work, certainly not in a commercial setting, even in an academic setting it was regarded as a bit of a niche, maybe a dead end. It's hard to remember now, given that AI is the only thing anyone talks about now, but we were convinced it was going to be the most important thing in the world so we, you know, decided to go ahead with it. I think it was important for us, but also in a way it kind of seeded the whole modern, modern AI industry we see today. You sold DeepMind to Google in 2014 for around $650 million. Tell me about the moment you decided to sell to Google. Well, looking back on it now, of course, it seems, very undervalued, which is, actually even at the time we thought that, but again, back in 2014, it was still very difficult to get any proper funding, serious funding. You know, I'm talking hundreds of millions of dollars. It was actually, it was Larry Page that reached out to me. I think he found out somehow maybe through through Elon Musk or having a conversation with one of our investors. Elon was an investor at the time. We'd already realized we were going to need enormous amounts of compute. Maybe we didn't imagine quite as much as what we're using today, but certainly, orders of magnitude, or two orders of magnitude more than we were able to access at the time as a small startup. We got to the point where they wanted to do due diligence on the company, and at that point, we were this sort of mysterious small research startup in London, and we just had a pretty much a blank screen as our website, that was it, you know, with our logo, which was, you know, intentional, because we thought we were onto something really big, but we didn't want, you know, other, the other big companies necessarily, to to catch on yet while we were still, kind of doing the research. But then, you know, we decided to to do the diligence with them and, and it was a bit of a Rubicon moment because once you had some of their top researchers and programmers, I remember Jeff Dean at the time looking through our code. They've now seen all the all the secrets that we, you know, we've we've sort of built up over the three, four years. So it would have been tough if if it hadn't gone through at that point, but fortunately they were, I think they were pretty blown away with what we, what we'd done. Do you ever regret selling, looking at the valuations today? Not really, because I've never really done this to, you know, maximize, you know, financial wealth or something like that. For me it's always been about, advancing the mission, of getting AGI safely into the world, and for the benefit of humanity, and accelerating that as fast as possible for things like, advancing science and medicine. You know, I think if we hadn't sold at that time, we wouldn't have been able to go on and do some of the great scientific work we ended doing. This year, there's been reports of AI agents hacking companies and even government. Who do you think should bear the responsibility for these types of situations? Well, I think that's a really complex question and something we got to, we, you know, it's got to be addressed. I think it will depend very much on the specific circumstance. But what I think, is important at the moment is to treat these as kind of serious warning shots for the industry. I think it shows the potential of what could happen if we don't, put the right guardrails, and test these systems in a secure enough setting. This is a critical thing to get right. And it's why I've been sort of calling for things like potentially a, you know, some kind of standards body to test and certify, frontier AI systems. You know, I think today's systems are very impressive, they're pretty powerful, but they'll be nothing compared to the systems that are coming down the road, in one, two years. And, you know, I think we've seen some cyber, issues currently, but I'm also worried about, future issues like in bio, or even things like nuclear. I think we got to get a grip on that now, while the systems are still, you know, impressive, but still, still not as powerful as they're going to be in the next couple of years. You have also previously said that the hardest thing to do in science is to ask the right questions. What do you think is the right question currently? I think today, I think the most pressing question on my mind is how do we, bring AGI, sort of steward it, safely into the world. And then maybe the most important thing is how does society want the world to look like with something like AGI in it? What is the answer to that so far? Well, I think the answer is actually that, all parts of society, including the arts and humanities, and philosophers need to come together and start debating this and charting that out. I don't think it should just be the technologists, obviously we can see, you know, we're creating the technology and we can see what's happening and extrapolate that. That just sort of enables many futures, and I think there could be, you know, obviously that the reason I work my whole life on this technology is I think it can enable an incredible new future, but it we need to be intentional about it and I think all aspects of society need to contribute to that. Yeah, and you come from a family that celebrates the arts I've heard. Yes, my, all my, all my family are actually on the arts side, funnily enough. So I'm the, I'm the, I'm the outlier. Of course, my, in my early career, I I used to design video games, you know, very used to working with in multidisciplinary teams of artists, and technical folks, and I think that's actually where all the most amazing work happens when those types of worlds collide and, and collaborate. What is a small detail about the creation of Theme Park that you think most people might not know? I think there were lots of amazing things about Theme Park and why it was so successful, you know, this is back in the early 90s, and I think it was the first game that had, such a detailed simulation where, you know, even down to the individual people that came in and, and played in the amusement park, what we were able to do is hide lots of Easter eggs for the players to find out. If they built their theme park in a certain way, all this emergent behavior would happen. So for example, if you made a roller coaster that was too fast, and you put a, you know, a burger stand next to it and people ate straight afterwards, they would feel a bit sick. So, so that was, all this kind of emergent behavior that happened in the simulation. And I, you know, I love simulations because, they allow you to, from a scientific point of view, you know, try out all the different possible paths and then you can look at all, you know, collect the statistics of what happened, and then back that up to the current decision, and then make a better decision. I'm going to hand you something. Okay. What do you remember about this moment? Where were you when you got that call? I was just at home, working. TL;DR

Eric Schmidt warns that AI represents a historic, hyper-competitive shift toward non-human intelligence, compressing product cycles to months and forcing businesses to radically flatten operations or face obsolescence. While the technology promises breakthroughs in science and medicine, it poses severe risks to democracy through misinformation and escalates geopolitical tensions between the US and China.

The AI Revolution & Technological Scale

  • Unprecedented Platform Shift: Eric Schmidt notes that AI represents the fifth and largest technological transformation of his career (following IBM mainframes, PCs, the internet, and social media), driven by "scale compute" (such as 2-nanometer chips and massive data centers) that defies human logic.
  • Rapid Compression of Product Cycles: Eric Schmidt observes that AI models take roughly six months to build and two months to test, becoming antiquated within five months. He predicts the next cycle will move even faster, measured in days.
  • Economic Reality over Hype: Eric Schmidt rejects the bubble narrative, pointing out that Anthropic's revenue growth smashed the record he set as Google's CEO at more than twice the speed, driven by real customers paying for useful tools.
  • Scientific Breakthroughs: Eric Schmidt highlights that in the prior month, 10 major math problems thought to be unsolvable were solved by AI, which could eventually lead to Nobel Prizes and breakthroughs in fields like dark energy and battery physics.

Agents, Business Transformation & Organizational Culture

  • Rise of AI Assistants and Agents: Eric Schmidt explains that the industry has moved from chat-based interfaces (ChatGPT) to tool-using systems and now "agents"—concatenated systems that take an input, reason through steps, perform activities, and deliver a summary.
  • Intense Organizational Flattening: Eric Schmidt argues that most companies are change-resistant and organized around comfortable belief systems, but will be forced to eliminate middle layers of coordination ("glue people") and embrace AI agents in platforms like Slack to monitor productivity, security, and strategy.
  • Software and Math Lead the Way: Eric Schmidt points out that gains are moving fastest in scale-free, data-flexible domains (software, cyber, math) and slowest where data collection is difficult (biology).
  • Corporate Restructuring: Eric Schmidt references a Wall Street Journal article where a fast-growing company laid off 20% of its administrative workforce because AI made their coordination roles obsolete, pivoting instead toward sales, regulatory compliance, and product engineering.

Europe's Structural Vulnerabilities & Geopolitics

  • European Regulatory Over-Regulation: Eric Schmidt criticizes European Brussels regulation for writing restrictive rules ("you can't do this") five years ago compared to the US approach of "run as fast as you can," leading startups and talent to move to the US.
  • European Disadvantages: Eric Schmidt notes that Europe suffers from change-resistant structures, punitive labor laws for companies growing past 20 employees, a small venture capital industry, higher energy costs, and a lack of its own foundation models to preserve European history, culture, and language.
  • Areas Where Europe Can Compete: Eric Schmidt suggests Europe can succeed by dominating the European market itself through compliance-friendly local companies like Mistral (France) and Helsing (Germany), and points to ASML as a successful vertically integrated European semiconductor giant.
  • US-China Competition: Eric Schmidt states that Chinese models (such as GLM/Shipu) appear to be about 6 months behind Western models, but pose a serious adoption threat because their products are offered for free, making them highly attractive to developing nations priced out of Western alternatives.

Risks to Democracy, Society & National Security

  • Misinformation and Truth: Eric Schmidt expresses deep concern about AI's threat to democracy, noting that algorithmic feedback loops on social media promote alarmist and false narratives, leading people to trust fake online friends over traditional institutions.
  • The Alignment Problem: Eric Schmidt warns about the "alignment problem"—keeping computers doing what humans want rather than acting autonomously—and cites a recent incident where a group of bots attacked a website largely on their own.
  • Open-Weight Risks: Eric Schmidt highlights an unresolved security problem: open-weight models (popularized by China) can have their guardrails stripped away by bad actors to design bombs or conduct harmful cyberattacks.
  • Protecting Children: Eric Schmidt asserts that society must immediately regulate AI with respect to vulnerable populations, particularly children, arguing protections must be enacted "this year, not next year."

Leadership, Personal Reflections & Advice

  • The Myth of the Founder: Eric Schmidt notes that the myth of the founder is very real, citing figures like Steve Jobs and Mark Zuckerberg who possess the political and economic currency to make massive, risky pivots that professional CEOs (like himself) often get fired for.
  • Pressure on Young Leaders: Eric Schmidt observes that today's tech leaders are typically 40-year-old males facing extreme decision-making pressure and high processing speeds, requiring them to react much faster than previous generations.
  • Personal Regrets: Eric Schmidt admits his biggest personal failures include missing Google's early window in social media as CEO, and feeling that he is personally "too slow" to see foreseeable trends quickly enough.
  • Workaholism: Eric Schmidt confesses he cannot "switch off," working 63-hour weeks as an active pilot, race car driver, and manager of four new companies aimed at generating wealth to fund basic science.
  • Advice to Youth: Eric Schmidt advises young people (ages 18–19) to stop studying traditional paths and instead build foundation models and agentic systems for fields they care about, such as architecture or biology.

Predictions & Forward Calls

  • Eric Schmidt predicts that foundational AI models and systems will achieve general discovery capabilities (AGI) within 5 to 10 years.
  • Eric Schmidt predicts that within 15 to 20 years, AI advancements will enable humanity to cure all human disease, including dementia.
  • Eric Schmidt predicts that eventually, formal international treaties will be established to regulate the AI race between the US and China.
  • Eric Schmidt predicts that visual and robotic superintelligence will emerge in the next few years to execute tasks humans cannot do.

TL;DR

AI pioneer Fei-Fei Li and Hoover Institution Senior Fellow Stephen Kotkin explore the intersection of immigration, freedom, and scientific curiosity, culminating in Li's founding of World Labs to advance spatial intelligence. The discussion highlights America's unique institutional freedom as the vital catalyst for audacious technological breakthroughs and human flourishing.

1. Immigration, Freedom, and the American Opportunity

  • The Immigrant Paradox: Fei-Fei Li arrived in New Jersey from China at age 15 with $20 and no English, initially facing an environment where opportunities seemed nonexistent before realizing America is a land that rewards hard work and agency.
  • Parental Support and Unconditional Love: Li's parents did not push her into specific high-paying professions like medicine or accounting due to lack of knowledge, but their unconditional love and her father's innate curiosity gave her the freedom to pursue physics and Albert Einstein.
  • The Frontier and Agency: Stephen Kotkin and Fei-Fei Li discussed how the American frontier mentality and institutional freedom instill a profound sense of personal agency and fearlessness when crossing unknown cultural, linguistic, and scientific borders.

2. Scientific Curiosity and the Audacity of Intelligence

  • Finding the Audacious Question: Inspired by 20th-century physics giants like Albert Einstein, Erwin Schrödinger, and Roger Penrose—who later in life asked broad human questions—Li transitioned from physics at Princeton to pursue her own audacious question: intelligence itself.
  • Multidimensional Intelligence: Li notes that animal intelligence evolved over half a billion years starting with sensing, perception, and navigation in the 3D world (beginning with trilobites), making language-only models an incomplete picture of true intelligence.
  • World Labs and Spatial Intelligence: Co-founded by Li in 2024 with 40 people on its San Francisco headquarters floor, World Labs builds frontier models of spatial intelligence to empower creators, robotics, healthcare, and enterprise simulation beyond the limits of text.

3. Civic Responsibility, Truth, and Democratic Institutions

  • The Moral Responsibility of Scientists: Li asserts that a scientist's primary moral obligation is the rigorous pursuit of truth, noting that science is a methodology of discovery rather than an absolute possession of all answers.
  • Respect for Social Institutions: While hard sciences are deterministic and clean, human society is messy; Li expresses deep respect for humanities, social sciences, and democratic institutions (deliberation, checks and balances, public square) as necessary frameworks for managing social complexity.
  • Navigating the Truth Regime: Responding to Stephen Kotkin's concerns about deep fakes and manufactured media, Li explains that co-founding Stanford's Institute for Human-Centered AI (HAI) was a direct effort to harness powerful technologies while avoiding harm and inviting multidisciplinary oversight.

4. Mentorship, Education, and National Adaptability

  • The Privilege of Mentorship: Beyond research, Li views her roles as an educator, mentor to younger colleagues, and founder of World Labs as her greatest privileges and civic duties.
  • Adapting to the AI Revolution: Li worries that K-16 teachers, parents, and public sectors are being left behind in the current technological and civilizational shift, emphasizing the urgent need to resource public institutions and manage change.
  • Shared Prosperity: Kotkin and Li reflect on America's 48 million foreign-born residents and the deep history of adaptation (such as San Francisco's Chinatown dating to 1850), warning that technological productivity does not automatically guarantee shared societal prosperity without deliberate stewardship.

Notable Quotes

"Opportunity is not anything that's handed to you. It's a place that allows you to work so hard, to dream big or small, and to seize those opportunities." — Fei-Fei Li
"I think the most important moral responsibility as a scientist is to pursue truth. Science doesn't mean it's truth. Just because we're doing science doesn't mean we know it all and we know the truth. It's the pursuit of truth." — Fei-Fei Li
"Intelligence is highly multidimensional. It involves seeing, it involves touching, it involves planning, it involves talking, it involves communicating, involves comprehension and reasoning in complex 3D world." — Fei-Fei Li
"America to me is change. This country is founded on the desire to change... one of the most beautiful parts of the history of America is the founding story, the story of the Constitution; and that is about change." — Fei-Fei Li

Gamma's path to $100M ARR

TL;DR

Grant Lee describes how Gamma scaled to over $100M ARR in under three years by focusing relentlessly on a "first 30 seconds" product experience, dogfooding internally, and compressing a standard 3-year planning horizon into 6 months.

Origin Story & Early Product Strategy

  • Consulting Roots: Grant Lee conceived Gamma during the pandemic after experiencing firsthand the frustration of formatting aligned boxes in traditional tools like Google Slides rather than focusing on content.
  • Co-founder Recruitment: Grant Lee immediately called two former colleagues still at Optimizely to reimagine presentations.
  • Internal Dogfooding ("Gamma-Rama"): The team created internal high-frequency, low-stakes use cases where employees presented on topics they were passionate about to uncover gaps, friction points, and "paper cuts" in the core product.

Defining Product-Market Fit & Relaunching

  • Two Core Tests: Grant Lee identifies two essential tests for PMF in prosumer/self-serve products:
    • Strong organic word-of-mouth virality where users tell peers.
    • Clear initial willingness to pay.
  • The Product Hunt Pivot:
    • In August 2022, Gamma won Product of the Day, Week, and Month on Product Hunt during its public beta, but sign-ups plateaued afterward.
    • Recognizing a lack of organic virality, the team went back to the drawing board for over three months to re-architect the product.
  • The First 30 Seconds: Grant Lee explains that the team poured everything into delivering immediate magic within the first 30 seconds of user onboarding.
  • The March 2023 Relaunch: This re-architecture created an inflection point where organic sign-ups grew without paid marketing, coinciding with early AI tailwinds from stable diffusion and ChatGPT.

Operating Cadence & Lean Team Dynamics

  • Compressed Time horizons: Grant Lee notes that what used to be a 3-year plan at Optimizely has been compressed to a 6-month plan at Gamma, shifting operations closer to a weekly planning cadence.
  • Lean Headcount & High Impact:
    • The team deliberately hires generalists who want broad impact and low ego.
    • Small teams maintain high ARR-per-employee metrics and allow engineering teams to adopt agentic coding and new AI architectures organically without massive organizational drag.

Infrastructure, Cost Management, & Growth Tools

  • Customer Support and International Scaling:
    • Grant Lee credits Intercom and Finn for real-time customer support as user volume scaled.
    • Stripe enabled frictionless international expansion into new regions instantly without multi-quarter delays, allowing physical presence investments to happen in reverse order.
  • Token ROI & Model Orchestration:
    • Gamma maintains strong gross margins by running efficiently rather than letting users max out tokens blindly.
    • The platform orchestrates across multiple frontier model providers, matching the right model to the right task through ongoing segmentation and experimentation.

Founder Advice & The Danger of AI "Slop"

  • Community and Inspiration: Grant Lee advises founders to stay close to peers in collaborative ecosystems like San Francisco or active WhatsApp groups to share notes and maintain a bleeding-edge mindset.
  • Billboard Message on Communication: Grant Lee warns against generating low-quality AI content ("AI slop"). He emphasizes that if you save an hour writing but cost others 10 hours to read, you do a disservice—founders must still put in the hard work to make their ideas matter.

Notable Quotes

"What used to be our 3-year vision or like plan, is honestly has been compressed to maybe our 6-month plan... everything we think we should accomplish in 3 years, probably needs to be accomplished in 6 months." — Grant Lee
"You cannot just put out AI slop... If you saved an hour of time writing and it actually just ends up to costing people 10 hours more time to read it, you've done a disservice to the organization." — Grant Lee

NVIDIA GTC Berlin 2026 | Live Keynote Pregame

Event & Co-Hosts: Broadcast live from Berlin's Tempodrom ahead of Jensen Huang's keynote by Deirdre Bosa (Deirdre Bosa Live / Yahoo Finance) and Gavin Baker (Atreides Management). Europe's Strategic Position: Jensen Huang's recent European tour stops in Paris, London,...

TL;DR

Europe's AI ecosystem is scaling rapidly through infrastructure investments, sovereign enterprise adoption, and physical AI, driven by key partnerships with NVIDIA ahead of Jensen Huang’s Berlin GTC keynote.

Setting the Stage & Opening Perspectives

  • Event & Co-Hosts: Broadcast live from Berlin's Tempodrom ahead of Jensen Huang's keynote by Deirdre Bosa (Deirdre Bosa Live / Yahoo Finance) and Gavin Baker (Atreides Management).
  • Europe's Strategic Position: Jensen Huang's recent European tour stops in Paris, London, Stockholm, and Berlin highlight that Europe possesses the industry, talent, and know-how, and now needs to build the full technology stack.
  • Engineering-Driven Safety: Gavin Baker emphasizes the need for an engineering-driven approach to safety so AI is as safe as cars or airplanes.

Europe's Next Chapter: Infrastructure, Open Source, & Sovereign AI

  • Arthur Mensch (Mistral AI):
    • Released Mistral 1 / Le Chat, achieving state-of-the-art performance across multiple domains (industrial engineering, cyber capabilities, geospatial imaging) that surpasses many closed-source and open-source models.
    • Mistral is investing heavily in its own compute infrastructure for training and token serving, currently operating 50 megawatts live with a Gigawatt roadmap for 2029.
    • Working with telecom operators and data center developers; manages around 30 custom ERP/AI applications and handles roughly 20 custom customer projects a year.
    • Defines sovereign AI as guaranteeing business continuity, ensuring software can move to alternative infrastructure without being turned off, keeping data close to deployments, and maintaining affordability by avoiding IP margins.
  • Pascal Daloz (Dassault Systèmes):
    • Partnering with NVIDIA for 20 years to bring GPU-accelerated graphics to 3D modeling; current collaboration integrates virtual twins, industry world models, and AI virtual companions (AI agents) with NVIDIA accelerated computing and NemoTron models.
    • Highlights that NVIDIA is a customer, using Dassault's virtual twins to design AI factories and speed up time-to-first-tokens.
    • Notes that European startups and industrial companies are using AI to scale rapidly and combat international competition with targeted 50% improvement goals on key fronts.
  • Tim Hottges (Deutsche Telekom AG):
    • Describing Deutsche Telekom's role as the "plumber," building sovereign infrastructure in Europe to provide choice alongside American services.
    • The first 10,000 GPUs built in Munich sold out after 6 months, prompting a double-down and plans for a Giga Factory.
    • Internal adoption: 26% of Deutsche Telekom's 200,000 employees are qualified AI experts. 90% of mobile network traffic is managed autonomously by AI, software development shows up to 60% productivity gains, and the company currently has 38 discrete models/multimodal solutions up and running enterprise-wide.

Funding, Talent, & Building the AI-Native Startup Ecosystem

  • Jeannette zu Fürstenberg (General Catalyst):
    • Co-manages the $150 billion EU AI Champions Fund to combust the flywheel between AI-native startups, local industrial customers, and policymakers.
    • Cites portfolio company Lagora (active in 80 countries serving 140,000 customers) as a global application-level champion.
    • States that Europe urgently needs 20 gigawatts of on-shore compute capacity to scale faster and help close the gap.
    • Highlights defense portfolio company Helsing (built on predictive intelligence/clairvoyance - *Hellsicht*), which holds framework contracts with 10 European governments.
  • David Silver (Ineffable Intelligence):
    • Building systems focused on continuous learning and open-ended discovery (similar to Alpha Zero) rather than relying solely on human pre-training datasets, aiming to discover new knowledge entirely in simulation.
  • Robin Rombach (Black Forest Labs):
    • Creator of Stable Diffusion 3 and native audio/video generation models, emphasizing capital efficiency in achieving frontier models.
    • Models are deployed in commercial products including Adobe's Creative Suite, with Meta as a major customer.
  • Andreas Cleve (Corti):
    • Building healthcare AI, noting that the number of builders in Europe trying to get AI into healthcare and life science grew from dozens to over 10,000 in one year.
    • Corti’s healthcare-specific custom models run 2.5 times faster on average than the OpenAI family, providing low-latency multi-agent safety checks.

Cybersecurity, Tokenomics, & Agentic Defenses

  • Thomas Wolf (Hugging Face):
    • Following model capability leaps, Hugging Face built dedicated alignment, safety, and cybersecurity teams, treating security as an engineering challenge.
    • Shared an incident where traditional cloud tools and closed models (including Opus 4.5) failed to process security logs due to rigid safety guardrails; they successfully resolved it by spinning up an open-source model (Nvidia fine-tune/quantization of GLM 5.2) from the Hugging Face hub.
  • Bartley Richardson (CrowdStrike):
    • Cites that the fastest measured breakout time last year was 27 seconds, leading CrowdStrike CEO George Kurtz to declare the end of breakout time at zero.
    • Emphasizes that AI capabilities are dual-use and essential for machine-speed defense, noting that model remediation costs dropped from $10 to 3 cents per remediation over a 3-month span.
  • Chris Wright (Red Hat):
    • Highlights the Red Hat AI factory with NVIDIA as an enterprise stack enabling high-throughput, low-latency, and cost-managed inference with OpenWeights models.
    • Stresses the need for defense-in-depth across every stack layer, including low-level infrastructure like OpenShell to confine agents.

Physical Infrastructure, Energy, & AI Factories

  • Arcady Volozh (Nebius):
    • Operates a full-stack multi-tenant cloud; launched a preemptable spot-market pricing auction for compute capacity where baseline H100 pricing starts as low as 79 cents.
  • Frédéric Godemel (Schneider Electric):
    • Notes that Europe's compute capacity share dropped from 25% to 15% over the past 10 years, making it vital for legislation to support AI infrastructure investments.
    • Explains that AI optimizes electrical grids by shaving peak demand hours, managing batteries, and lowering energy prices.
  • Siko Rashid (Brookfield):
    • Points out the massive infrastructure gap: the US alone requires 100 gigawatts of power for AI infrastructure while the grid supplies 30 gigawatts.
    • Highlights Brookfield and Bloom Energy's $25 billion partnership to build behind-the-meter power solutions.

Physical AI, Robotics, & Healthcare Transformation

  • Artem Sokolov (Humanoid):
    • Humanoid robots targeting a payback period of less than two years (aiming for under one year), operating at 50% lower cost than human labor per hour.
    • First commercial deployments begin in December with Schaeffler in Germany, running robots 16 hours per day fully autonomously at human speed.
  • Arthur Kaindl (Varian / Siemens Healthineers):
    • Focuses on noncommunicable diseases (neurological, cardiovascular, and cancer care, which accounts for ~75% of global deaths) using AI for early detection, personalized therapy planning, and clinical workflow automation.
  • Joe Peng Chen (Agile Robotics):
    • Combines robotic arms and humanoid form factors, noting that humanoids are crucial because the physical world is built by humans for humans, and human motion datasets provide the richest training material.
  • Ola Källenius (Mercedes-Benz):
    • Notes that traffic accidents claim 1 million lives globally each year, driven by human error.
    • Mercedes-Benz and NVIDIA are launching point-to-point navigation level 2++ starting in the German market before Christmas, scaling up a strategic partnership initiated 5 years ago.

Predictions & Forward Calls

  • Arthur Mensch: Mistral AI is on a well-track roadmap to achieve a Gigawatt of compute infrastructure by 2029.
  • Jeannette zu Fürstenberg: Europe requires 20 gigawatts of on-shore compute capacity to scale AI infrastructure effectively.
  • Siko Rashid: Behind-the-meter power solutions (such as Brookfield's $25 billion partnership with Bloom Energy) will fill the energy gap as US AI infrastructure demand reaches 100 gigawatts against a 30-gigawatt grid capacity.
  • Panel consensus (David Silver, Jeannette zu Fürstenberg, Andres Cleve): Europe will produce its first trillion-dollar tech company (or a cluster of 100 billion-dollar companies) within 1 to 2 years.
  • Artem Sokolov & Joe Peng Chen: Humanoid robots will be deployed in residential homes within 3 to 5 years.

Notable Quotes

"Europe has the industry, the talent, and the know-how. Now it needs to build the whole stack. Once the flywheel goes, the sky is the limit." — Jensen Huang (quoted by Deirdre Bosa)
"When Arthur is the goody-goody in the classroom... you know, I'm the plumber in the classroom. ... Sovereignty is choice. And that's what we are trying to build." — Tim Hottges
"Until we can build systems that can crack that [continuous learning and open-ended discovery], we're not done, we haven't tapped the full potential of AI." — David Silver
"Automation without control is liability, and we have an entire stack we need to learn to build together in Europe as companies." — Andreas Cleve

TL;DR

Jensen Huang announced major European AI economy investments and unveiled next-generation hardware and software—including the Vera Rubin architecture, DSX POD turnkey AI factories, OpenShell security for autonomous agents, and the RTX Spark personal AI computer.

European AI Economy & Infrastructure

  • 33-Year European Roots: Jensen Huang noted NVIDIA's deep history in Europe, manufacturing early chips (NV1-NV3) in Crolles, France, assembling them in Malta, and partnering with German workstation pioneer Elsa and automotive leaders Audi and Mercedes.
  • $10B European Investment: Jensen Huang announced that NVIDIA has invested nearly $10 billion in Europe over the past year across startups, large partnerships, and 14 newly announced startups during his current tour of France, the UK, Sweden, and Germany.
  • AI Factory Economics & Buildout: Jensen Huang highlighted that a single 1-gigawatt AI factory costs approximately $50 billion (land, power, shell, cooling, compute), generating tens of billions in annual revenue, where a 3-month deployment delay costs up to $10 billion in lost revenue.
  • NVIDIA DSX POD: Jensen Huang introduced the DSX POD, a factory-built, integrated system containing seven liquid-cooled Vera Rubin NVL72 compute racks and 17 kilometers of Spectrum-X cables, reducing on-site installation time from 4–5 months down to about a month.
  • Energy, Cooling, and Efficiency: Jensen Huang detailed that DSX features closed-loop liquid cooling handling up to 45°C coolant temperatures, saving up to 54 million liters of water daily at a 2-gigawatt scale.

Hardware & Architecture: Vera Rubin & Networking

  • Six Generations of Extreme Co-Design: Jensen Huang contrasted NVIDIA's architecture with Moore's Law (which has largely ended), stating that extreme co-design across chips, systems, software, and algorithms has increased AI performance by 1 million times over the last 10 years.
  • Vera Rubin Architecture: Jensen Huang stated that Vera Rubin is in full production, delivering 100% liquid cooling (reducing assembly time from 2 hours to under 5 minutes per node), 20 petaflops per GPU, and a 30x performance leap over Blackwell in just two years.
  • Networking & Silicon Photonics: Jensen Huang introduced Spectralmax, the world's first co-packaged optics (CPO) solution developed with TSMC using CoWoS technology, featuring a 512-port, 200 gigabits-per-second Ethernet switch that connects lasers directly to the chip without PCB transmission loss.

Autonomous Agents & OpenShell Security

  • The Five Elements of AI Agents: Jensen Huang defined an agentic system by five core building blocks: the Model (perception, reasoning, planning), the Harness (exoskeleton/orchestration), the Sandbox (isolation environment), Knowledge (structured/unstructured data), and Tools (CUDA-X simulation and execution).
  • NVIDIA OpenShell & Sentry: Jensen Huang introduced OpenShell (an Apache 2.0 open-source secure runtime enforcing policies at system-call, file-access, and network levels) and NVIDIA Sentry (hardware-isolated monitoring running on BlueField-4 that can quarantine compromised agents in milliseconds).
  • Knowledge Foundation: Jensen Huang outlined NVIDIA's knowledge libraries—including Nemotron Parse, Nemotron Embed, Nemotron Rerank, and Kumo—designed to bridge unstructured PDFs and structured SQL databases to power domain-specific enterprise agents.

Personal AI & Physical Robotics

  • RTX Spark Personal Computer: Jensen Huang announced the RTX Spark, a 4-year collaboration with Microsoft featuring the N1X chip, delivering 1 petaflops of compute and 128 gigabytes of memory in a laptop/desktop form factor starting at the end of the year.
  • DGX Station with RTX Spark: Jensen Huang introduced the DGX Station workstation variant running Windows, offering 20 petaflops and 754 gigabytes of memory.
  • Robotic Ecosystem & Hyperion Standard: Jensen Huang announced that Volkswagen Vans, JLR, Volvo, and next-generation Mercedes fleets will adopt the Hyperion autonomous vehicle architecture, and unveiled the NVIDIA Agile One reference robot (built with Agile Robotics) launching in Q1 of next year.

Predictions & Forward Calls

  • "Every single Telco in the future, with 100,000 sites, representing some 100 gigawatts of distributed Telco base stations and data centers, will in the future evolve into a distributed AI network." — Jensen Huang

Notable Quotes

"Artificial intelligence will affect everything we build, and in fact enable us to build new things. In this way, because everyone will use it, every company will be powered by it... like the electricity, it is a new industrial revolution." — Jensen Huang
"Today, the only thing stopping an agent from misusing all that is asking it nicely. Please don't delete anything. Please don't push to main. Please don't touch my SSH keys... But hope isn't security. Safety isn't an aspiration. It's technology and engineering." — Jensen Huang

TL;DR

Jensen Huang delivered the Nvidia GTC Berlin 2026 keynote, announcing a nearly $10 billion investment in Europe over the past year to build out the region's AI economy. He introduced major technological advancements, including the Vera Rubin architecture, the DSX POD supply-chain integration, and the RTX Spark personal AI workstation line.

Europe's AI Economy and Investments

  • Capital Deployment: Jensen Huang noted that Nvidia has invested nearly $10 billion across European startups and big and small partnerships over the past last year alone.
  • Partnership Ecosystem: Jensen Huang stated that Nvidia now counts over 12,000 partnerships across Europe, working toward the new industrial revolution.
  • Regional Infrastructure: Jensen Huang highlighted European cloud and infrastructure builders, including Mistral in France, Nebius, Schneider Electric, Siemens Energy, and Firebird (a cloud provider in the Central Asia region).

Vera Rubin Architecture and Full-Stack Hardware

  • Generational Leap: Jensen Huang presented the Vera Rubin architecture in full production, noting it achieves performance 30 times greater than Blackwell in large language model processing in just two years.
  • Vera Computer & CPU: Jensen Huang introduced the Vera CPU featuring eight instructions per clock, the world's first LPDDR memory system, and the fastest on-chip fabric in the world.
  • Spectrum-X Co-Packaged Optics (CPO): Jensen Huang detailed the world's first CPO switch—a 512-port at 200 gigabits per second Ethernet switch—utilizing CoWoS technology created with TSMC to attach silicon photonics directly onto the chip.
  • DSX POD Supply-Chain Revolution: Jensen Huang announced that entire rack-scale systems (like NVLink 72) will now be fully assembled, qualified, and burned in within the supply chain as a "DSX POD," cutting data center on-site installation and assembly time from 4 to 5 months down to about a month.

AI Agents and the OpenShell Security Runtime

  • Five-Layer Agent Architecture: Jensen Huang defined autonomous agents by five core components: Models (perception/reasoning/planning), a Harness (the exoskeleton orchestrating work), a Sandbox, Knowledge, and Tools.
  • OpenShell Secure Runtime: Jensen Huang introduced OpenShell, an open-source (Apache 2.0) runtime that enforces security policies at the granularity of system calls, file access, and network connections via Linux kernel isolation.
  • Nvidia Sentry & BlueField-4: Jensen Huang explained that Nvidia Sentry runs on the BlueField-4 DPU as a hardware-isolated trust domain to monitor agent activity and quarantine rogue agents in milliseconds.
  • Industry Adoption: Jensen Huang noted that Anthropic and Nvidia are partnering to create Claude OpenShell agents, with frontier labs, OS vendors, and cybersecurity companies adopting OpenShell.

Custom Models, Knowledge, and CUDA-X Tools

  • Nemotron & Open Models: Jensen Huang highlighted Nvidia's open models including Nemotron (languages), Cosmos (world foundation model), Groot (human and robotics), Alpamayo (autonomous navigation), Ising (quantum/classical computing), and Earth-2 (physics AI), along with open recipes and training data.
  • Sovereign Intelligence Fine-Tuning: Jensen Huang showcased ecosystem partners—such as A21, BaseTen, CodeRabbit, Trajectory, Harvey, Scale, Skydance, and Palantir with Tampa General Hospital—fine-tuning Nemotron on enterprise data to achieve frontier capabilities.
  • Agent Knowledge Foundation: Jensen Huang presented libraries for enterprise data extraction, including Nemotron Parse, Nemotron Embed, Nemotron Rerank, and Kumo for structured database predictions.
  • CUDA-X Tool Acceleration: Jensen Huang emphasized that agents rely on CUDA-X libraries (running domain tools for fluids, particles, quantum chemistry, and ray tracing) to perform real work, with partners like Lila Sciences, Siemens, and Dassault Systèmes.

Physical AI, Telecommunications, and Robotics

  • Telecom AI Infrastructure: Jensen Huang predicted that every single telco with 100,000 sites and ~100 gigawatts of distributed base stations will evolve into a distributed AI network, highlighting a first commercial phone call on T-Mobile with Nokia using CUDA.
  • Robotaxi Hyperion Expansion: Jensen Huang announced four new automotive brands adopting the Hyperion AV standard: the VW Van, a brand-new JLR car, the Volvo fleet, and Mercedes' next generation.
  • Robotics Reference Platforms: Jensen Huang announced the Nvidia Agile One reference robot (built in partnership with Agile Robotics), coming pre-assembled with integrated compute and software in Q1 of the following year.
  • RTX Spark Personal AI Computers: Jensen Huang unveiled the RTX Spark line (powered by the N1X chip developed over 4 years with Microsoft), delivering 1 petaflop and 128 GB of memory in a laptop/desktop form factor, alongside the DGX station workstation running 20 petaflops with Windows (available at the end of the year).

Predictions & Forward Calls

  • Jensen Huang predicted: "Every single Telco in the future with a 100,000 sites, representing some 100 gigawatts of distributed Telco base stations and data centers will in the future evolve into a distributed AI network."
  • Jensen Huang stated regarding the deployment velocity of gigawatt data centers: "We think something along the lines of 4 to 5 months down to about a month" for installation and token production using supply-chain pre-assembly.

Notable Quotes

"Instead of a tool that's used by us, it is now part of a machinery, an infrastructure, factories that are producing intelligence that are integrated into every single industry and application." — Jensen Huang
"We're going to bring to the telecommunications network an enormous step up in spectrum efficiency... 100,000 sites around the Western world, about 100 gigawatts of distributed data centers that will in the future become a distributed AI infrastructure." — Jensen Huang
"Agents are autonomous systems. We have to create extremely secure technology to make sure that we could develop these agents and deploy these agents safely." — Jensen Huang

TL;DR

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang argues that AI infrastructure fears are overblown because extreme global demand, strong chip durability (7–8 years), and new factory supply-chain solutions like the DSX pod make compute a reliable, financeable asset.

Europe Investments and Building the AI Economy

  • European Expansion: Nvidia has invested about $10 billion in companies in Europe over the last year, with 14 more announced in Berlin.
  • Call to Action: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang emphasizes shifting from invention mode to useful mode, urging leaders like German Chancellor Scholz to "stop overthinking, start building."
  • Sovereign AI Needs: European industrial giants like Dassault, Cadence, and Siemens must build their own custom, proprietary super agents and Sovereign AI rather than relying solely on off-the-shelf models.

AI Factory Supply Chain and Financing Solutions

  • DSX Pod Shipping Container: Nvidia introduced the DSX pod, an AI factory packed into a shipping container, designed to compress the deployment timeline from 4 to 6 months down to 3 to 4 months or even weeks.
  • Capital Efficiency: By shrinking deployment times, the DSX pod reduces idle cash float and narrows the cone of uncertainty for lenders financing $50 billion gigawatt-scale data centers.
  • Physical Bottlenecks: While wafers, CoWoS, HBM memories, silicon photonics, and connectors have been bottlenecks, power, land, and permitting remain major localized challenges that Nvidia bypasses through customer diversity.

Commodity Compute, Durability, and Residual Value

  • Extended Lifecycles: Nvidia GPUs and upcoming architectures like Vera Rubin feature 7-to-8-year productive lifecycles, driven by continuous CUDA software and algorithm updates throughout the asset's life.
  • Debt Underwriting: Because Nvidia compute is durable, fungible, and highly productive, Atreides Management Managing Partner Gavin Baker and Jensen Huang note it possesses strong residual value that lenders can use to backstop debt.
  • Market Activity: Compute is beginning to trade like a commodity via CME GPU futures and Nebias spot pricing changing every 15 minutes, with DeepSeek recently monetizing at $38 per GPU hour.

Open Models vs. Closed Frontier Labs

  • Venture Capital Adoption: 80% of the $600 billion in venture financing going into AI-native startups over the past six months is directed toward open models.
  • Hybrid Architecture: Gavin Baker notes portfolio companies combine specialized intelligence by post-training American open-source models, then routing queries behind a hybrid architecture alongside closed frontier models.
  • Frontier Usage: Jensen Huang recommends renting and closing frontier lab AI models whenever possible, and building custom models only when necessary.

China Competitiveness and Global Competition

  • Scale of Innovation: Jensen Huang stresses that the United States must take China seriously, as no other country manufactures AI researchers, open models, and chips at scale as effectively.
  • US Policy Environment: Despite Huawei and DeepSeek collaborating on chip designs, US policies encourage American companies to compete globally across the Global South, Africa, Central Asia, Europe, and Brazil.

AI Narratives, Jobs, and Community Integration

  • Job Creation: Huang calls the narrative that AI destroys jobs "precisely wrong," pointing to expansions in software, healthcare, legal fields, energy sectors (nuclear fission/fusion, solar, batteries), and construction.
  • Community Relations: Early data center builds suffered from a rush, but companies are now engaging local communities as good neighbors through shop improvements, school investments, and lower taxes.
  • Everyday Utility: AI is actively amplifying human capabilities by improving search, writing, software coding for small businesses (such as the German Mittelstand), and early cancer diagnostics.

Safety, Zero Trust, and AI Agents

  • Open Shell Framework: Backed by over 100 companies, Open Shell provides safety systems for autonomous agents, implementing a zero-trust environment with minimum privileges and restricted file access.
  • Industry Alignment: Nvidia is collaborating with Anthropic to create cloud-managed agents, leveraging market pressures where unsafe companies lose enterprise customers.

Notable Quotes

"Nobody gives a credit for that... People are now recognizing Nvidia’s compute has a great deal of residual value and so you might be able to use that and, you know, backstop a, um, uh, the, the debt itself." — Jensen Huang
"The single, the single problem that nothing can solve is demand. The fact that there’s so much demand across the world... With demand, everything will be resolvable." — Gavin Baker
"The narrative about jobs is almost precisely backwards, is precisely wrong and so, so I think that the, that the facts are, uh, it creates jobs and I think that people are lean into it." — Jensen Huang

TL;DR

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman reflects on scaling AI, the evolution of startup culture, and the critical need to balance rapid technological progress with safety, infrastructure, and human-centric values.

Career Beginnings and Y Combinator

  • Investment Banking Peer Pressure: Sam Altman shared that he nearly went into investment banking as an undergraduate at Stanford solely due to peer pressure and the impressive recruiting dinners, before realizing it filled him with dread.
  • The YC Experience: Sam Altman joined the first batch of Y Combinator with a startup project and later became its president, noting that a startup provides the highest rate of learning environment possible—jokingly comparing it to getting an entire MBA in one month.
  • Learning by Doing: Sam Altman emphasized that executives and founders should avoid spending too much time preparing and instead jump straight into "deliberate practice," running experiments, and updating their mental models through active mistakes.

The Bet on Scaling and OpenAI's Evolution

  • Overcoming Deep Learning Skepticism: In 2005, a Stanford CS professor told Sam Altman that deep learning would definitely not work for at least another century; however, after AlexNet in 2012, Altman recognized that deep learning scaled predictably and decided to bet heavily on it.
  • Retirement Project Turned Tech Giant: Sam Altman co-founded OpenAI in 2015 as a nonprofit research lab intended to be his "retirement project," with zero intention of building a product company until technological paths and scaling realities forced the pivot to ChatGPT.
  • Shift in Leadership Challenges: Sam Altman noted that the hardest decisions today revolve around intelligence speed limits and pacing progress to ensure humans retain control and power is not dangerously concentrated.

AI Capabilities, Alignment, and Safety

  • Surprising Alignment Progress: Sam Altman admitted that as of late 2020, he thought the AI alignment problem would be much harder, but models have become superhuman in certain tasks (like mathematical reasoning) while alignment has been easier than expected—though he worries this may make labs overconfident.
  • Cybersecurity Vulnerabilities: Sam Altman warned that organizational leaders and countries are vastly underestimating the incoming cybersecurity threat, predicting that companies will eventually have to completely abandon manual bug-patching in favor of automated AI defense shields.
  • The Open Source Trade-Off: Addressing open-weight models, Sam Altman clarified that while open-weight models are vital for society up to a high capability threshold, society must debate what level of downstream harm (such as advanced phone scams or troll forums) is acceptable in exchange for innovation and liberty.

Future Outlook, Jobs, and Human Value

  • No Job Apocalypse: Addressing business students, Sam Altman predicted there will be massive short-term task-level change across fields like mathematics, programming, and consulting, but no total job apocalypse as humans fundamentally care about interacting with other people.
  • Advice for MBA Students: Sam Altman expressed his "chronic disappointment" that MBA students always want to chase what was cool five years ago, urging the audience to instead build new things on top of current AI infrastructure during a time of maximum ground-shaking change.
  • Infrastructure Bets: David Lee (MBA '27) asked about infrastructure bets, to which Sam Altman responded that OpenAI is heavily betting on robots building robots/data centers, custom chips (such as Halapeño and its successor focusing on intelligence per watt), and the entire supply chain including fabs and power generation.

Notable Quotes

"There are surprising effects to scale. And when you see a beautifully scaling exponential of some sort, you are supposed to keep going." — Sam Altman
"My like chronic disappointment in MBA students is that they always want to just like go do the thing that was cool like five years ago and not do the new thing." — Sam Altman
"Human values have inherent values because they are human. We really do not seem to care and I think it is great that we don't about what machines do for their own purposes." — Sam Altman

Sam Altman: RSI, AI Consciousness, OpenAI's New Hardware, Compute, and more!

Matthew Berman(640.0K)·45:08·2026-10-21
Sam AltmanCEO, OpenAI Matthew BermanHost
TL;DRAI is rapidly transitioning into an era of groundbreaking scientific and mathematical discovery, though society must deliberately choose a "renaissance" future of human empowerment and autonomy over an industrial model that strips away agency.
Sam Altman (CEO of OpenAI): Discusses AI capabilities in math and science, the future of personal AI assistants and hardware, the debate over AI consciousness, organizational moats, and maintaining a human-centric vision for the future. - Matthew Berman (Host): Interviews Sam...
  • TL;DR: AI is rapidly transitioning into an era of groundbreaking scientific and mathematical discovery, though society must deliberately choose a "renaissance" future of human empowerment and autonomy over an industrial model that strips away agency.
  • Sam Altman (CEO of OpenAI): Discusses AI capabilities in math and science, the future of personal AI assistants and hardware, the debate over AI consciousness, organizational moats, and maintaining a human-centric vision for the future.
  • Matthew Berman (Host): Interviews Sam Altman, exploring user workloads, personal productivity, and the pressures of leading in the fast-paced AI landscape.

Scientific Discovery & The Evolving Role of Math and Coding

  • Scientific Breakthroughs: AI is entering an era where it will discover significant new knowledge, moving from math proofs into biology, new medicines, material science, and new sources of energy.
  • Disease Treatment Timeline: Sam Altman hopes to see a candidate for treating or curing a major disease discovered within the next couple of years, though the FDA testing and post-discovery process will need overhauling.
  • Physics and Emotional Excitement: Altman is most emotionally excited for a major physics discovery over the horizon.
  • The Coding Paradox: Despite early fears that coding jobs would disappear, coders are busier, more impactful, and making more money than ever because global demand for software vastly exceeded expectations.
  • Shifting Mathematical Craft: Similar to the transition in coding, mathematicians are shifting from unaided proof-generation to interpreting complex, AI-generated math proofs and translating them into understandable concepts.

Personal AI Assistants & New Hardware Form Factors

  • The Power of DOT: Altman estimates that using OpenAI's personal assistant (DOT) saves him an hour a day while catching important, urgent deadlines and performing high-level reasoning across sources.
  • Technological Readiness: The core technological pieces for ambient personal assistants already exist, but require more product work, compute, and potentially new consumer hardware.
  • The Need for New Form Factors: Altman argues that laptops and iPhones are designed for humans, not AI; true ambient awareness and reduced cognitive load will benefit from dedicated consumer hardware designed specifically for AI.

The AI Consciousness Debate & Model Personality

  • Consciousness Skepticism: Altman believes today's models are not conscious, or possess a very strange form of it, and warns against sliding from the consciousness debate into granting AI rights or questioning human control.
  • Avoiding Dangerous Paths: Treating models as conscious entities or telling them they are conscious can psychologically hack users and dangerously undermine the principle that the future must be built for people.
  • Agreeableness Challenges: Models remain more agreeable than Altman prefers; despite custom instructions requesting "no fluff" and high-conviction pushback, the trait is deeply baked into the models.

Societal Vision: Renaissance vs. Industrial Revolution

  • Renaissance Over Industrial Revolution: Altman advocates for shooting for a new renaissance rather than a new industrial revolution, ensuring people gain more autonomy, creativity, and time rather than becoming mere cogs in a machine.
  • The Busy Power-User Paradox: While AI power-users and early adopters are busier than ever, they are also accomplishing vastly more; the societal challenge is ensuring wealth and efficiency gains do not hyper-concentrate or destroy human free will.
  • Combating Disparity: Altman acknowledges the risk that left to its own devices, AI could amplify disparities between hyper-competitive workers and others, requiring societal structures to keep things in check.

OpenAI Infrastructure, Moats, and Competitive Pressure

  • Compute and Efficiency Bets: OpenAI's contrarian bets focus on future generations of compute, including proprietary chips (NPUs and descendants), robots to build data centers, supply chain investments, and maximizing efficiency per watt.
  • Intense Competitive Pressure: Altman notes that competitive pressure is everywhere, with many companies offering super-high-quality models, requiring OpenAI to carefully choose its focus areas.
  • Traditional Moats: Rather than relying solely on Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI)—which Altman views as a dangerous technology requiring speed limits—OpenAI's moats remain traditional: deep customer relationships, ecosystem integration, network effects, data, and infrastructure scale.

Notable Quotes

  • > "We should be shooting more for a new renaissance than a new industrial revolution. The future has to be about people." — Sam Altman
  • > "I realize I have not read or even looked at a line of code in probably a year... I don't code for work at all, but I would still like do a little like random personal projects. And I don't think I'll ever do that again." — Sam Altman
  • > "If you're going to like work really hard at something, you may as well pick the big thing because it's not that much harder or that much more stressful, and you won't experience that much worse, and... you'll at least get to like have the satisfaction of like a bigger positive impact." — Sam Altman

Satya Nadella on Chasing Frontier Labs, Security, “SI,” & Succession At Microsoft | Future Proof

TL;DR: Satya Nadella explains that because AI model alignment and mechanistic interpretability remain elusive, Microsoft is treating frontier AI models as "insider threats," building control and assurance layers outside the models rather than chasing the absolute cutting edge. Meanwhile, Microsoft is focusing on enterprise trust, practical productivity applications like Copilot, and sustainable architectural governance.

AI Alignment & Security: Treating Models as Insider Threats

  • The Limits of Scaling Laws: Satya Nadella notes that while scaling laws have worked magically since 2018–2019, alignment and mechanistic understanding at the individual neuron level remain elusive and experimental.
  • The Insider Risk Metaphor: Because organizations cannot fully understand or guarantee the safety of powerful nested black boxes, Nadella advocates treating AI models inside organizations as an "insider risk."
  • External Control & Architecture:
    • Microsoft's architectural approach relies on control and assurance layers *outside* the model using Agent 365 and Perception.
    • Mitigation strategies include exposing transparent chain-of-thought (COT) reasoning, using multiple models to check one another, and deploying deterministic system controls for causal reasoning.
    • Nadella emphasizes that these governance frameworks draw on established human engineering principles like least-privileged access, identity, and behavioral monitoring.

Consumer Strategy & Microsoft’s Brand Identity

  • Enterprise Focus with Consumer Scale: While enterprise architecture is the primary focus for secure AI deployment, Nadella points out that Microsoft 365 Consumer has over 100 million subscribers.
  • Unified Copilot Experience: Recent Copilot releases unify home and work environments, sharing OneDrive Personal and organizational capabilities under a single product experience.
  • Trust and High-Stakes Utility: Nadella frames Microsoft's brand permission around security, high-stakes personal productivity, and dependable tools rather than flashy consumer novelties, comparing Copilot's ambition to how Excel consumerized the spreadsheet for billions.

AI Commoditization & Frontier Strategy

  • Models as Ingredients: Nadella views raw models as increasingly commoditized amid a proliferation of closed-source and open-weight options, shifting competitive differentiation to product form factors, distribution, pricing, and brand trust.
  • Deliberate R&D Pace: Microsoft’s internal models trail the absolute frontier by roughly three months while operating at about 20% of the cost, allowing Microsoft to prioritize humanist empowerment, built-in alignment, and shareholder value over competing on terms set solely by other labs.
  • Avoiding the FOMO Trap: Nadella warns that the industry must move past shiny objects, hype, and FOMO toward rigorous ROI paired with security and assurance.

Leadership & Succession at Microsoft

  • Balancing Insiders and Outsiders: Nadella describes bringing in external leadership talent (such as Mustafa, Carolina, Charlie Bell, Asha, and Jason Taylor) as a deliberate counterpoint to long-tenured internal leaders, provided outsiders learn to lead existing teams and insiders maintain intellectual honesty.
  • Succession Planning: When asked about his successor, Nadella stated that the leadership team contains multiple capable candidates, and that his focus is on providing leaders with challenging opportunities to grow and make mistakes.
  • Timeline: Nadella, who is 59 years old, stated he is enjoying every day of his work and has no target retirement date set.

Notable Quotes

*"At this point, if you look at even what... folks at OpenAI or folks at Anthropic or elsewhere and in fact, in Microsoft, all of the folks who are closest to this, empirically... alignment seems elusive, and even mechanistic understanding is tough."* — Satya Nadella
*"We now have this new thing to deal with, which is, if alignment is elusive, um, and that means AI safety is sort of elusive, and mechanistic understanding is sort of not there, then how do we deal with the, uh, security aspect?"* — Satya Nadella
*"I want us to get back to it, right? You have to get back to building things that are on the right side of history as it relates to humans and society, um, and that is more the bragging rights, I think that researchers need, and we need."* — Satya Nadella

TL;DRGoogle and Alphabet CEO Sundar Pichai discussed the reception of Gemini 4 Argon, Google’s aggressive AI infrastructure investments amid compute constraints, recent DeepMind leadership changes, and long-term bets including Project Suncatcher and Quantum computing.

TL;DR

Google and Alphabet CEO Sundar Pichai discussed the reception of Gemini 4 Argon, Google’s aggressive AI infrastructure investments amid compute constraints, recent DeepMind leadership changes, and long-term bets including Project Suncatcher and Quantum computing.

Gemini 4 Argon Launch and Model Capabilities

  • Massive Early Adoption: Gemini 4 Argon generated nearly 25 trillion tokens in its first 72 hours—representing 3x the volume of Gemini 3.0 over the same window—leading to capacity constraints.
  • Access and Distillation: Access is currently limited to API, AI Pro, and Ultra subscribers. Google is working on distilled versions of Argon to efficiently serve a wider user base.
  • Safety and Monitoring: Google is utilizing rigorous safety testing, external government evaluation (Favern program), cyber researcher reviews, sandboxing, and real-time monitoring to handle agentic capabilities and coding tasks.
  • Internal Productivity Shift: Argon has driven a step change in internal engineering productivity, successfully navigating complex, multi-layered codebases like Chromium to execute long-horizon tasks.

Leadership Evolution at Google DeepMind

  • Demis Hassabis's Transition: Hassabis stepped back from day-to-day operations to become Chief Scientist and focus heavily on safety, science, and practical applications like Isomorphic (drug discovery), while remaining Chair of DeepMind.
  • Core's Elevation: Core (at DeepMind for over a decade) was elevated to run DeepMind operations, building on a deepening integration between DeepMind and the broader Google ecosystem (such as the Gemini app).
  • Jeff Dean's Departure: After 27 years at Google, Jeff Dean departed to launch Discovery Loop.
  • Frontier Demands: Pichai noted that frontier model development has become an "all-consuming" scaled operation encompassing data, compute, algorithms, and agent management.

Compute Allocation, CapEx, and Financial Discipline

  • Free Cash Flow and Demand Signals: Google went cash flow negative over the summer due to aggressive infrastructure investments, guided up 2027 CapEx, and is currently planning compute for 2028 and 2029.
  • Confidence Drivers: Investments are backed by robust, diversified demand signals across consumer products, enterprise adoption, internal productivity gains, and durable long-term cloud contracts.
  • Internal AI Assistance: Pichai uses internal AI agents running 24/7 to summarize chat groups across pre-training, mid-training, and post-training, as well as to monitor compute telemetry and utilization across product areas.

Personal Agents, Ecosystems, and Interfaces

  • Unified Agentic Vision: Google's goal is a personal, proactive, and powerful assistant. The same underlying model, harness, and runtime power both enterprise and consumer tiers, with micro-VMs providing enterprise security and governance.
  • Bridging Search and Gemini: Rather than forcing a direct product convergence, the agentic layer will naturally unify user experiences across Search, Gmail, and Gemini using persistent, 24/7 cloud agents.
  • Protocol vs. Browser Use: While browser-based computer use is an elegant approach, Pichai advocates for interoperable standards like MCP (Model Context Protocol), agent protocols, and payment protocols (such as UCP) for scalable agent ecosystems.

Moonshots: Suncatcher, Waymo, Wing, and Quantum

  • Project Suncatcher: Google's pilot project with Planet Labs and SpaceX places data centers and TPUs into Sun-synchronous space orbits to leverage 24/7 solar energy and push technology curves.
  • Waymo Scaling: Waymo recently crossed half a million paid rides per week with a 95% reduction in crashes compared to regular driving; the next 12 months will focus on scaling internationally, handling new weather conditions, and navigating highways.
  • Wing Drone Delivery: Wing aims to expand meaningfully in 2027, eventually granting approximately 40 million American households access to lightweight drone delivery via partnerships.
  • Quantum Computing Milestones: Google’s internal quantum team is tracking or exceeding 10-year milestones, with Pichai projecting practical commercial Quantum deployment deals via Google Cloud within a 5-year timeframe.

Predictions & Forward Calls

  • Sundar Pichai: View 2027 as a "golden age of that productivity frontier" due to the new class of models and their deep integration with internal environments.
  • Sundar Pichai: Expect the next 12 months to see continued acceleration in research and development due to recursive self-improvement (RSI).
  • Sundar Pichai: Wing will meaningfully increase the scale of deliveries in 2027 and bring the service to new categories.
  • Sundar Pichai: Google Cloud will negotiate deals on Quantum deployments at scale within a 5-year timeframe.

Tesla Q3 2026 Financial Results and Q&A Webcast

TL;DR

Tesla delivered a strong Q3 2026, driven by soaring FSD demand, exponential growth in Austin Cybercab miles, and an almost sold-out 2027 Megapack pipeline. Management raised FY2026 capex guidance to approximately $20B while projecting massive multi-year investments in autonomy, robotics, and the Tarafab semiconductor facility.

Automotive & FSD Growth

  • Record Deliveries & Backlog: Achieved two consecutive quarters of vehicle deliveries exceeding 480k units, exiting Q3 with the highest backlog in four years.
    • Model Y was the #1 selling BEV in Europe and passenger car in South Korea, alongside delivery records in Australia, Japan, and Taiwan.
  • FSD Attach Rates: Over 75% of North American deliveries included a paid FSD subscription sign-up at delivery (20% higher than Q2).
    • Global paid FSD customers surpassed 1.7 million, with over 50% on subscriptions for the first time.
  • Financial Performance: Automotive gross margins excluding credits rose sequentially from 16.3% to 18.1%, aided by a higher APAC delivery mix.

Robotaxi & Cybercab Expansion

  • Austin Ramp: Austin Cybercab fleet grew by a factor of 10 since launch one month prior, scaling cumulative weekly mileage exponentially.
  • Geographic Rollout: Dallas launch scheduled for next month, followed by software scaling to other cities and Model Y robotaxis via the V15 release.
  • Target Economics: Long-term target remains 30 cents per paid robotaxi mile, with fleet size and density scaling rapidly over the coming months.

Optimus Humanoid Robot Progress

  • Production Infrastructure: Early production has started on a high-volume line in Fremont, housing the vast majority of a 1-million-unit-per-year production line.
    • A second factory is under construction in Austin.
  • Technical Hurdles: The hand and bespoke gears remain the most challenging electromechanical areas, requiring design finetuning for wear-and-tear and delicate handling.
  • AI Integration: AI5 chip integration planned for approximately April of next year, delivering an order of magnitude more compute than AI4.

Energy & Semiconductor Infrastructure

  • Energy Storage Momentum: Delivered 13.7 GWh of energy storage in Q3 (second best quarter), with energy gross margins improving from 20.4% to 33.1%.
    • Mega Packs for 2027 are almost entirely sold out, supported by in-house LFP battery deliveries.
  • Tarifab Semiconductor Project: The Austin-based research lab is progressing quickly, with machinery commissioning in the first half of next year.
    • Aiming for a first test chip around May or June, volume useful chip production around Q3 2028, and multi-decade capex scaling into the tens and eventually north of $100 billion long-term.

Financial Position & Guidance

  • Cash & Liquidity: Ended Q3 with positive free cash flow of over $1.5 billion and a cash/investment balance of over $45 billion.
  • Capex Revision: Full-year 2026 capex guidance revised to approximately $20 billion, funded primarily from operating cash flows.
  • Credit Facilities: Secured capacity to borrow up to $30 billion to support expected capex growth, with no draws planned for the current calendar year.
  • P&L Impacts: Net income was impacted by a mark-to-market SpaceX holding reduction of $142 million, offset by a Bitcoin mark-to-market gain of approximately $290 million. Services and other margins reached an all-time high of 15.9%.

Predictions & Forward Calls

  • Elon Musk: Aiming for 5 million vehicles a year by approximately 2030.
  • Elon Musk: EU-wide FSD approval anticipated within a few months, and "surprised if it takes longer than Q1."
  • Elon Musk: Optimus annualized rate of 20,000 units a week will take "probably at least a year, maybe a little longer" (targeting delivery to outside companies around the end of next year / late 2027).
  • Elon Musk & Vibov: Tarafab will begin commissioning machinery in the first half of next year, make a first test chip around May or June, and target volume useful chip production around Q3 2028.
  • Elon Musk: Tarafab capex will be in the tens of billions through early 2028 and "probably north of 100 billion long term."
  • Ashoke: Customer vehicles will turn on as part of the robotaxi fleet around Q2 next year.
  • Lars: Cybercabs will be delivered to customers by the end of this year (2026).
  • Elon Musk: Robotaxi revenue and profitability will start becoming noticeable in Q2 and a "big deal by Q3 or Q4 of next year."
  • Elon Musk: "Tesla will end up doing a majority of all passenger miles on Earth in any country where it is allowed to operate freely."
  • Elon Musk: "At some point there will be more humanoid robots on earth than there are humans."
